title: Man, And Cybercrime
affiliations: Dallas college

detail.title: Man, And Cybercrime

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research received no external funding.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Cybercrime has become one of the most significant challenges facing contemporary society as digital technologies continue to expand across all sectors. While traditional cybersecurity approaches have primarily focused on technological vulnerabilities, research increasingly demonstrates that human factors play a critical role in both cybercriminal activities and cyber victimization. This paper examines the psychological, social, and behavioral aspects of cybercrime through a review of relevant theories and empirical literature. Particular attention is given to cybercriminal motivations, victim susceptibility, social engineering techniques, organizational cybersecurity behavior, and the growing influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on cybercrime trends. The paper adopts the Theory of Planned Behavior, Social Learning Theory, Health Belief Model, and Space Transition Theory as theoretical foundations for understanding human behavior in cyberspace. The study concludes that effective cybersecurity requires a multidisciplinary approach that combines technological safeguards with humancentered interventions, awareness programs, and behavioral security practices.

title: Governance Before Action: Institutional Authority for Agentic AI in Banking

detail.title: Governance Before Action: Institutional Authority for Agentic AI in Banking
detail.abstract: The deployment of frontier AI models into regulated financial institutions has created a governance problem that existing supervisory frameworks were not designed to answer. Recent regulatory developments distinguish deterministic rulebased systems from statistical models while simultaneously recognizing that generative and agentic AI require new governance approaches. The result is not a lack of regulation, but an unresolved architectural question: where should institutional authority reside when probabilistic models participate in regulated decisions? This paper argues that institutional authority should remain outside the model. Rather than allowing frontier models to interpret regulatory obligations directly, regulated actions should be authorized through an independently governed determination layer that evaluates machine-readable obligations, institutional policies, permissions, and verified facts before any consequential action is executed. Models remain responsible for interpretation, retrieval, explanation, and orchestration, but they do not become the institution's source of authority. The paper defines the architectural properties required of such a determination layer, proposes a supervisory examination framework based on replayable determination records rather than behavioral observation alone, and identifies an empirical research agenda for comparing determination-layer architectures against model-centric approaches. It reports conformance evidence from a working implementation as an existence proof that these requirements are simultaneously satisfiable and machine-checkable; no comparative results are claimed. It further argues that this architecture naturally produces the evidence artifacts increasingly expected by supervisors while preserving human accountability over institutional judgment. The author discloses a commercial interest as the founder of GOLDAi, whose prototype implements elements of the proposed architecture, and as the named inventor on a pending United States patent application covering aspects of the architecture described in this paper. The architectural thesis advanced here should be evaluated independently of the pending patent application and any commercial implementation.

title: A Speech-Centred Systems Framework for Human-AI Adaptation and Economic Coordination

detail.title: A Speech-Centred Systems Framework for Human-AI Adaptation and Economic Coordination
detail.abstract: Economic models of human behaviour systematically underrepresent speech-the primary medium through which agents process information, coordinate meaning, and manage uncertainty. This paper proposes a Speech-Centred-Systems-Framework in which speech acts are treated as measurable state variables linking individual cognition, interpersonal negotiation, and institutional outcomes. The framework adapts Cognitive Load (CL; Sweller 1988) and introduces three formal constructs-Meaning Load (ML), Containment Availability (CA), and Net Meaning Stress (NMS)-specifying how they interact, asymmetrically across agents, to shape outcomes across six multi-scale layers. A constitutive-versus-diagnostic speech distinction prevents conflating speechas-experienced with speech-as-measured. The primary contribution is operationalising Meaning Load-previously an unmeasured theoretical concept-as a reliable, CFA-validated linguistic metric deployable as an economic state variable (CFI = 0.924; RMSEA = 0.083). Empirical validation uses two complementary corpora (laboratory and marketplace negotiations). Testing ML as a standalone behavioural constraint against competing hypotheses drawn from standard economic theory-communication as costless cheap talk (Crawford & Sobel 1982) versus communication as linear transmission cost-the data reject both: Meaning Load functions as an engagement signal in platform-mediated negotiations (OR = 10.82, p < .001), predicting deal completion rather than failure. The asymmetric discounting mechanism predicted by extending Rubinstein-style models receives no empirical support, demonstrating that the costly-meaning assumption does not hold in asynchronous marketplace settings. A stylised state-transition model illustrates how constitutive speech expands the action space beyond parameter modification. The framework preserves orthodox economic foundations while explaining persistent asymmetries in participation, negotiation outcomes, and institutional legitimacy without invoking irrationality or moral preferences.

title: Attestation, Not Detection: An Authenticity Substrate for Ubiquitous AI

detail.title: Attestation, Not Detection: An Authenticity Substrate for Ubiquitous AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher who develops AI-verification technology and has a commercial interest in the domain this paper concerns. The author has filed pending U.S. provisional patent applications covering the hardware-rooted per-output attestation, per-turn session-continuity, and recipient-edge verification mechanisms described in this paper. As the paper states, that commercial interest lies in the product layer and not in the neutral root of trust the paper argues must remain a non-commercial public utility. The argument is offered on its merits and stands independently of the author's interest. No other competing interests are declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual position paper. It involves no human participants, patients, personal data, or animal subjects, so ethics approval and participant consent are not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author, who is an independent researcher.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes cheap and ubiquitous, ordinary people are losing the ability to hold an AI interaction to an accountable source — to tell an authentic, answerable system from an impersonated, tampered, or anonymous one — and no amount of good intent by honest developers repairs this, because the problem is adversarial and the population cannot be made vigilant at scale. The instinctive response, detection — classifiers that spot AI content — is not merely failing but provably unwinnable: the best possible detector's accuracy decays toward chance as machine and human outputs converge (Sadasivan et al., 2023), a limit already visible in the retirement of production detectors and their demographic bias (OpenAI, 2023; Liang et al., 2023). This paper argues that the answer is not detection but attestation: an infrastructure that makes an authentic, accountable AI interaction cryptographically provable, and treats the unattested as suspect by default. The existing forms attest the wrong unit — provenance attests files (C2PA), confidential computing attests the compute (trusted execution environments), and regulation mandates self-disclosure (EU AI Act, Article 50) — while the unit that matters, the live interaction, goes unclaimed, and the hardware to secure it does not yet exist. Grounding the proposal in the pattern by which trust has repeatedly migrated into the substrate — HTTPS, code signing, and Certificate Transparency succeeded; DNSSEC stalled — the paper specifies a six-part substrate and then locates its decisive problem, enforcement, at the network layer, where registration would become a precondition of connection. It is here that the paper turns from proposal to reckoning. The network is the only chokepoint with the reach to make the unattested illegitimate; it is also the architecture of the national firewall, it presupposes a neutral root of trust that may be an empty category, and it fights a free-rider gradient that its closest precedent — RPKI, whose enforcement reaches only 12.3% of networks after a decade — shows failing. These are not reasons to abandon the substrate. They are the four problems — the binding, the root, the gradient, and the censorship equivalence — that must be solved before it is built, because the alternative to building it deliberately is having it built, badly or malignly, by the crisis or the state that reaches the chokepoint first. Its own resolution is to place enforcement not at the network's core but at the recipient's edge — real exclusion, but recipient-chosen and plural-rooted, which escapes the censorship architecture — and to be candid that the market will not summon even this, since the historical record shows lucrative trust-gated transactions reliably pulling in cheaper substitutes (reputation, insurance, tokenization, walled gardens) rather than attestation; so the trust layer must be willed into being at a client-edge chokepoint, the way Chrome forced encryption, rather than waited for. The paper delivers accountability, not the stronger discernment its subject might imply, and argues for confronting these problems early — before the collapse of shared epistemic ground forces a worse answer.

title: Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation: Human-Routed External Verification Without Inter-Model Deliberation

detail.title: Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation: Human-Routed External Verification Without Inter-Model Deliberation
detail.abstract: When multiple large language models are consulted on the same question, agreement is often treated as evidence of reliability. That inference is weak when models share training data, development pipelines, or alignment methods, and a divergence-triggered procedure cannot address identical correlated errors. This paper isolates a narrower, tractable object: the procedural interval between visible inter-model divergence and final decision. We develop Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation (OMT), a low-machinery verification procedure. Models are queried separately, without access to one another's outputs and without debate, critique, or synthesis. Their divergences are preserved and classified before cross-exposure. A human observer selects decision-relevant divergences and routes each, by type, to grounding independent of the output chain under review. The verification chain ends with the return of grounding, not a synthesized verdict; final adoption is a separate, recorded human judgment. OMT retains five authorities on the human side: salience, routing, sufficiency, stopping, and final adoption. Each is assigned to a named decision-maker, with dispositions and stated grounds recorded. Cases with no observed divergence, or no selected divergence, close as screening prefixes and do not certify agreement. Because the observer is fallible, the method requires observation-condition logging and, in repeated deployment, an error-model ledger that includes both human and model failure modes. The paper defines the constitutive conditions, verification stages, provenance requirements, risk tiers, and failure modes of OMT. Four author-reported development episodes motivate the framework but do not validate it. OMT does not claim superiority over deliberation protocols or improved decision accuracy. Its designed contribution is narrower: to make the path from divergence to external grounding, and from grounding to adoption, attributable and inspectable.

title: Transforming Waste Management Through Artificial Intelligence: A Multi-Theoretical Framework for Sustainable Innovation Adoption

detail.title: Transforming Waste Management Through Artificial Intelligence: A Multi-Theoretical Framework for Sustainable Innovation Adoption
detail.abstract: Contemporary municipal waste management systems face unprecedented challenges arising from exponential waste generation growth, resource depletion concerns, and mounting environmental pressures. This paper develops a comprehensive integrated theoretical framework that elucidates the complex mechanisms through which artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies influence adoption processes and operational outcomes in municipal waste management contexts. Drawing upon established theoretical foundations from Circular Economy Theory, Diffusion of Innovation Theory, Resource-Based View, and Stakeholder Theory, we construct a sophisticated multi-dimensional framework that identifies and systematizes three critical driver categories: technological, organizational, and environmental factors. Our theoretical contribution advances beyond existing fragmented approaches by establishing clear causal pathways linking specific AI capabilities to measurable operational efficiency gains and environmental sustainability outcomes through nine rigorously formulated empirically testable propositions. The manuscript provides detailed operational measurement protocols and comprehensive methodological guidance for empirical validation, addressing critical gaps in current scholarship. The primary contribution represents a theoretically grounded, empirically actionable roadmap for advancing systematic research and evidence-based policy analysis in the emerging domain of AI-enabled sustainable waste management systems.

title: From the Enlightenment to the Digital Dark Age: The Transfer of Epistemic Authority to Algorithms Without Understanding

detail.title: From the Enlightenment to the Digital Dark Age: The Transfer of Epistemic Authority to Algorithms Without Understanding

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: In 2026 a generative search system (Google Search), asked in sequence about failure rates in hyperscale artificial-intelligence datacenters, produced an extended, fluent, citation-laden account of graphics-processor error, silent data corruption, thermal warping, power transients, cooling failures, regulatory mandates, and emerging legal doctrine. A subsequent audit by a second frontier model (ChatGPT) found the account substantially unwarranted: a reverse-engineered failure rate presented as an industry constant, incompatible denominators, a category confusion inflated into a universal claim, a process node misstated, an invented international metric, misdescribed statutes, and demonstration code whose “corrupted” and “healthy” inputs were identical. That validation code is reproduced and executed in Appendix A, where it reports success while detecting nothing. This essay treats the episode as a documented specimen. It argues that the failure was not mechanical but epistemic, and that the two are separable: a hyperscale system can execute a defective reasoning process with near-perfect physical and computational fidelity. Distinguishing physical, computational, and epistemic integrity explains why additional compute alone cannot cure the defect, why the ubiquitous “this system may make mistakes” notice is non-diagnostic, and why generative search inverts the traditional division of epistemic labor—performing the synthesis while returning verification to the user. The essay locates the deeper source of the problem in an epistemic regression gradient present to varying degrees in most bodies of human knowledge but concealed within the system’s unified presentation, and proposes a counter-architecture: an open, laptop-resident small language model bound to a curated, provenance-preserving disciplinary corpus and governed by a human scholar under the Maestro Model. The proposal is offered not as an escape from epistemic uncertainty but as a disciplined way to inhabit it.

title: AI, Work and the Shape of the State: Rollout in the Public Sector and Private Sector

detail.title: AI, Work and the Shape of the State: Rollout in the Public Sector and Private Sector

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Independent research, no funder

detail.abstract: AI in the UK is a political economy issue, contrasting private sector labour substitution with public sector capacity enhancement to boost service quality. While the private sector focuses on margin expansion and potential job displacement to concentrate wealth in fewer hands, the public sector can leverage AI to reduce administrative tasks and empower staff, aiming to improve productivity in human-facing roles and enhancing social value. Moreover, if the disappearance of well-paid jobs in the private sector profoundly disrupts the labour market, diminishes the tax base and creates a pool of unemployed skilled workers, the public sector will need to step in by providing socially useful roles, most sensibly through a guaranteed job scheme.

title: Weaponized Trade Routes and Global Maritime Bottlenecks: An Econometric Assessment of Supply Chain Shocks and Resiliency Dynamics on Indian MSMEs
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Weaponized Trade Routes and Global Maritime Bottlenecks: An Econometric Assessment of Supply Chain Shocks and Resiliency Dynamics on Indian MSMEs
detail.abstract:
This paper provides an empirical investigation into the asymmetric vulnerabilities of Indian Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) amid rising geoeconomic fragmentation and the weaponization of critical global maritime trade routes. Utilizing a comprehensive econometric framework that combines structural gravity models with high-frequency shipping and firm-level customs and balance sheet data, this study evaluates how disruptions at vital maritime chokepoints-such as the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, and the Bab-el-Mandeb strait-propagate through international supply chains to affect resource-constrained enterprises in developing economies. 

Our findings reveal that maritime bottlenecks induce severe cost-push inflation and protracted transit delays, resulting in acute working capital squeezes and a structural contraction in export volumes for Indian MSMEs, particularly within labour-intensive sectors like textiles, leather, and light engineering goods. Furthermore, the econometric results demonstrate that firm-level export intensity, low balance sheet liquidity buffers, and the absence of financial hedging mechanisms significantly exacerbate vulnerability to exogenous shipping shocks. 

The study concludes with strategic policy recommendations, emphasizing the necessity of transitioning from rigid "just-in-time" paradigms to resilient "just-in-case" operational frameworks, alongside targeted liquidity management, digital trade facilitation, and proactive trade corridor diversification by policymakers and export promotion councils.

title: The Stanford EDGAR Filings Dataset: Reconstructing U.S. Corporate and Financial Disclosures into Layout-Faithful and Token-Efficient Pretraining Data
affiliations: UCLA Anderson, Nanjing University and Stanford University - Department of Management Science & Engineering

detail.title: The Stanford EDGAR Filings Dataset: Reconstructing U.S. Corporate and Financial Disclosures into Layout-Faithful and Token-Efficient Pretraining Data
detail.abstract: As high-quality public web corpora become increasingly exhausted, clean longcontext documents have become a scarce and expensive source of training data for large language models (LLMs). Existing long-context corpora are often proprietary and costly to acquire, synthetically generated, or concentrated in narrow domains such as programming. We introduce the Stanford EDGAR Filings Dataset (SEFD), an open reconstruction of SEC filings into layout-faithful MultiMarkdown for financial language modeling and evaluation. SEFD makes audited financial statements, risk disclosures, ownership reports, accounting notes, and market-moving event filings usable as long-context pretraining data and as a basis for financial reasoning, forecasting, compliance, and document understanding. The resulting corpus is token-efficient, model-ready, and has less than 0.1% overlap with Common Crawlderived corpora. We release SEFD-v1, a 152B-token initial public snapshot, and provide corpus-level analyses of a larger 18.5M-filing archive estimated at 550B tokens. We further introduce two SEFD-derived benchmarks: EDGAR-Forecast, which evaluates filing-grounded numerical forecasting after model knowledge cutoffs, and EDGAR-OCR, which evaluates transcription of complex financial tables.

title: Modelling Order Effects and Interference in Consumer Choice:A Quantum-Inspired Diagnostic Toolkit for Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis
affiliations: , Instituto Português de Administração e Marketing (IPAM), affiliation not provided to SSRN and Instituto Português de Administração e Marketing (IPAM)

detail.title: Modelling Order Effects and Interference in Consumer Choice:A Quantum-Inspired Diagnostic Toolkit for Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declares that there are no known financial, professional, institutional, or personal relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the development or presentation of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual and theoretical paper and did not involve human participants, animals, personal data, clinical data, or the collection of empirical data. Consequently, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required
declarations.funderStatement: The paper presents an independent conceptual and theoretical contribution and received no specific funding from public, commercial, or not-for-profit organisations

detail.abstract: Classical conjoint and discrete-choice models typically assume that consumer preferences are stable, pre-existing and independent of the context of elicitation. Behavioural evidence suggests instead that preferences are often constructed during evaluation and can be sensitive to the sequence in which attributes are considered. This paper advances a quantum-inspired diagnostic framework,  the Quantum-Conjoint Diagnostic Toolkit (QCDT),  that operationalises concepts from quantum probability theory, notably state representation, sequential projection and interference, within controlled choice-based conjoint experiments. Quantum probability is used here as a formal mathematical framework for context-dependent judgement, not as a claim about neural mechanism. We argue that when attributes are evaluated sequentially, the corresponding operations may be non-commutative, so that observed choice probabilities can depart from the classical law of total probability in a manner captured by an interference term. We present the conceptual model and a pre-registered protocol for an online choice experiment in which attribute-presentation order is counterbalanced while product information is held constant. Classical benchmarks (multinomial logit, mixed logit, hierarchical Bayes) will be compared with a quantum-inspired specification using out-of-sample prediction, information criteria and posterior predictive checks under a Bayesian workflow. The analysis plan, exclusion rules, stopping rule and interpretation grid are fixed in advance. The project is framed as Design Science Research: its principal artefact is a reusable, documented toolkit. A null result is treated as a substantive contribution, delineating the boundary conditions under which classical conjoint models are sufficient.

title: From Smart City Recognition to Data-Driven Smart Environment Governance: Evidence from Surabaya's Public Datasets and Policy Documents
affiliations: , Universitas Negeri Surabaya and Universitas Negeri Surabaya

detail.title: From Smart City Recognition to Data-Driven Smart Environment Governance: Evidence from Surabaya's Public Datasets and Policy Documents
detail.abstract: Surabaya is widely recognized for digital-service innovation and communitybased smart-city initiatives, yet less is known about whether its public data infrastructure supports evidence-based environmental governance. This study evaluates the availability, reusability, and policy alignment of Surabaya's public environmental data using an explanatory embedded single-case study. The evidence comprises 14 official datasets, the Surabaya Regional Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMD) 2021-2026, and relevant literature. A six-criterion governance rubric was combined with an unsupervised machinelearning-assisted semantic analysis. Dataset titles, descriptions, and visible metadata fields were represented alongside corresponding RPJMD passages using term frequencyinverse document frequency, reduced through Latent Semantic Analysis, and compared using cosine similarity across five model specifications. The semantic analysis revealed uneven correspondence between dataset metadata and RPJMD policy language. Alignment was strong for wastewater and sanitation (0.807), moderate for waste services (0.745), mobility and transport-related environmental pressure (0.650), urban resilience (0.637), and air quality (0.603), and weak for public green space (0.429). No similarity scores were available for drainage or energy conservation because no corresponding publicly traceable datasets were identified. The broader governance assessment also showed uneven maturity: air quality, waste, and sanitation had the most developed public-data coverage, while drainage, water quality, energy performance, and green-building performance remained poorly represented. The study contributes a reproducible dataset-to-policy crosswalk and an exploratory computational framework for evaluating smartenvironment data governance. The data, code, and analysis outputs used in this study are publicly available in the accompanying GitHub repository: https://github.com/rischanlab/rpjmd_surabaya_lsa

title: The Augmented Board: AI, Caremark, and the End of Episodic Oversight

detail.title: The Augmented Board: AI, Caremark, and the End of Episodic Oversight
detail.abstract: Two facts about AI and the board have arrived together. AI is accelerating strategic change beyond the cadence of episodic oversight, while AI-assisted research is sharply reducing the cost of keeping directors thickly informed. The result is the augmented board: not a board governed by AI, but directors who use it to become more deeply informed while keeping individual judgment and collective accountability. The paper defines that model through four properties: a common factual base, AI-assisted but independently exercised judgment, information that reaches the board when material facts change, and collective decisions supported by evidence. It situates the model in existing Delaware oversight doctrine and in recent cases on AI-assisted work, privilege, discovery, and evidence, without claiming that AI creates a separate fiduciary duty. It offers two practical disciplines: STAR as a recurring board review, and the Disclosure Mirror, which shows that the questions investors ask and the evidence a company must be able to show are the same list seen from opposite sides. The move is from episodic oversight and vibe governance to a board that can prove it governed.

title: Firm Performance and Textual Similarity between Sustainability Disclosure and Key Audit Matters: Evidence from NLP Analysis

detail.title: Firm Performance and Textual Similarity between Sustainability Disclosure and Key Audit Matters: Evidence from NLP Analysis
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the economic consequences of disclosure alignment by examining how the contextual similarity between KAMs and sustainability disclosures affects both current and future firm performance among Japanese listed companies. Focusing on the four key pillars of sustainability reporting (Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics & Targets), this study evaluates and compares the empirical insights of two NLP methodologies: Cosine Similarity and BERTScore. 
Using a comprehensive dataset of 1,194 Tokyo Stock Exchange entities for fiscal years 2024 and 2025, this study finds that while Cosine Similarity scores are consistently higher than BERTScores, they exhibit no statistically significant relationship with corporate performance across most dimensions, except for a marginal positive association within the "Governance" pillar under specific conditions. In contrast, empirical results using BERTScore reveal a positive relationship between future performance and contextual alignment within the "Metrics & Targets" pillar. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that BERTScore serves as a practical evaluation metric for corporate disclosure quality. Thus, this study establishes BERTScore as a valuable tool for assessing audit quality, voluntary disclosures, and sustainability integration.

title: Publikacja / Publication from Trademarks to Metabrands: How Coca-Cola, Mcdonald's and Meta Keep Winning the Glocal Game
affiliations: , Mackenzie Presbyterian University and

detail.title: Publikacja / Publication from Trademarks to Metabrands: How Coca-Cola, Mcdonald's and Meta Keep Winning the Glocal Game

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded in whole by the National Science Centre in Poland, grant “Brand Abuse: Brand as a New Personal Interest under the Polish Civil Code against an EU and US Backdrop”, grant holder: Marlena Maria Jankowska-Augustyn, number: 2021/43/B/HS5/01156. For the purpose of Open Access, the author has applied a CC-BY public copyright licence to any Author Accepted Manuscript (AAM) version arising from this submission.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the evolution of brand identity from traditional trademarks to contemporary "metabrands" in the context of digital transformation and glocalization. It argues that in the twenty-first-century global economy, brands operate simultaneously as legal assets, cultural icons, and digital platforms, requiring a delicate balance between global consistency and local responsiveness. Drawing on trademark law, cultural studies, and marketing scholarship, the study analyzes three emblematic case studies: Coca-Cola (confronting cultural heritage and indigenous rights claims over the coca leaf), McDonald's (mastering glocal adaptation through localized menus, franchising, and digital innovation), and Meta Platforms (navigating trademark conflicts arising from its high-profile rebranding). The chapter introduces the concept of the metabrand—a hybrid identity co-created by corporations, consumers, and communities—and explores the legal, cultural, and strategic implications of this shift. It concludes that effective brand stewardship in the digital glocal era requires integrating legal tools with cultural sensitivity and strategic agility, transforming intellectual property law from a regime of dominion to one of dialogue.

title: Derivatives on Compute: Pricing Theory and Market Design for AI Infrastructure

detail.title: Derivatives on Compute: Pricing Theory and Market Design for AI Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Compute is incresingly becoming an important input into the economy, and in many sectors it has earned its place alongside energy or labor. Like other production inputs, compute is exposed to volatile price risks. However, compute also exhibits unique characteristics that distinguish it from traditional commodities and must be addressed. Despite this, no standardized derivatives market yet exists to price compute or hedge its risks. This paper closes the gap by developing the mathematical framework and market architecture for standardizing compute derivatives, enabling the pricing, hedging and transfer of compute risks. We argue that compute behaves like a non-storable service commodity akin to electricity or freight rather than oil, and make the economic case for such a market via classical hedging-pressure theory. We address the prerequisite of an observable reference price by defining a quality-normalized benchmark, the Compute Reference Unit (CRU), model the CRU price as a mean-reverting jump-diffusion, and then derive closed-form futures, swap, and option prices and a physical risk premium within an incomplete-markets framework. We further quantify, against real hardware pricing data, the residual hardware-specific basis risk that quality normalization via the CRU necessarily leaves behind, and derive a model-implied minimum-variance hedge ratio for it. Worked numerical examples illustrate the framework throughout.

title: Is Public Capital Productive? Evidence from Major Bridge Collapses
affiliations: HEC Montreal, Alberta School of Business, University of Alberta, HEC Montreal and University of Virginia - Department of Economics

detail.title: Is Public Capital Productive? Evidence from Major Bridge Collapses
detail.abstract: We study whether public capital raises private-sector productivity by exploiting sudden, plausibly exogenous bridge collapses as localized losses of existing transportation infrastructure. We construct a novel dataset of 34 major U.S. bridge collapses over 1964--2024 and match these events to county-level manufacturing data. Local projections show that collapses reduce manufacturing labor productivity by 2--5 percent, with the trough occurring one year after the collapse, typically after the affected crossing has reopened. A county-economy model attributes the losses primarily to the disruption and gradual rebuilding of route-specific organizational capital, rather than to the direct loss of physical capital alone.

title: The P-Star Price Gap is Not Identified in Real Time

detail.title: The P-Star Price Gap is Not Identified in Real Time

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher and received no financial support for this work. The author has no personal, professional, or financial relationship with Peter Ireland, Stephen Miran, or Nouriel Roubini, and no affiliation with or financial interest in Hudson Bay Capital, the publisher of the paper under discussion. The analysis uses only publicly available data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED and ALFRED) and the Center for Financial Stability; the author has no affiliation with either institution. All code, data and figures required to reproduce every result are publicly available at github.com/josjo80/pstar-monetarism.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human participants, no animal subjects, and no personal or identifiable data. It is a computational reanalysis of publicly available aggregate macroeconomic and monetary time series published by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis and the Center for Financial Stability.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding. It was conducted independently by the author, without institutional, commercial, or grant support.

detail.abstract:
Ireland, Miran and Roubini (2026) revive the Hallman–Porter–Small (1991) P-star model, estimate it on Divisia monetary aggregates through 2026Q1, and conclude that the stance of monetary policy is “quite close to neutral,” that recent high inflation is therefore attributable to adverse supply shocks, and that the Federal Reserve should adopt a “wait and see” posture. I reproduce their Table 1 to within 0.02 on every coefficient and their reported potential-growth diagnostics to within 0.03 percentage points, then subject the framework to four tests they do not perform. First, I reconstruct the price gap from ALFRED vintages as a policymaker would have seen it at each date. The revision standard deviation is 3.13 percentage points against a gap whose own standard deviation is 2.88 — a noise-to-signal ratio of 1.09 — and real-time and hindsight estimates disagree on the sign of the policy stance in 33% of quarters. Applying this revision distribution, the 90% band on every one of their six 2026Q1 price gaps spans zero. The paper’s central quantitative claim is not identified in real time. The failure is almost entirely filter endpoint (revision sd 3.13) rather than data revision (0.31). Second, I locate the cause. The gap requires estimating two unobserved trends at the sample endpoint. Removing potential output (the nominal-GDP framing) achieves almost nothing; removing both trends by using 4-quarter money growth reduces noise-to-signal to 0.06 and real-time sign errors to zero, at no cost in predictive accuracy. An attempt to estimate equilibrium velocity structurally from CFS user-cost data across eight specifications fails: none is cointegrated (Engle–Granger ADF −1.68 to −2.17 against a 5% critical value of −3.34). Third, and most constructively, the problem is the filter rather than the price gap. The Hamilton (2018) regression filter dominates every HP variant on real-time reliability and predictive power simultaneously — noise-to-signal 0.24, sign errors 11%, standardised effect 0.356 against 0.267, out-of-sample RMSE gain over an AR(4) of 5.8% against 3.5%. Decisively, at 2021Q4 with inflation about to peak, the HP gap read +2.2 in real time against a hindsight value of +9.2, having decayed to neutral; the Hamilton gap read +18.7 against +21.8 and held the warning throughout. The paper’s own central historical claim — that money gave a usable advance warning of the post-2020 inflation — survives only under a filter it does not use. Fourth, I test the supply-shock attribution the paper asserts but never estimates. The price gap survives the addition of measured supply variables (γ rises slightly, to 0.093, HAC t = 2.76), so it is not a repackaged supply shock. But over 2025Q1–2026Q1 oil contributes +0.00pp because oil fell through 2025, while tariffs contribute +1.17pp of the +2.03pp rise in PCE inflation. The deglobalization half of the paper’s explanation holds; the energy half does not, for the window it is invoked to explain. Meanwhile 2026Q2 records the third-largest oil shock since 1946, implying +1.5 to +2.1pp on inflation by 2027Q1 — an order of magnitude larger than any monetary signal here, and arriving roughly a year earlier than the paper’s own hedge anticipated. On the paper’s preferred filter the current stance cannot be distinguished from neutral. On the better filter, two of six specifications clear zero — but their signal comes largely from the filter’s extrapolation of past velocity rather than from money, and the six specifications disagree far more than under HP, which undercuts the paper’s claim that the choice of aggregate “hardly matters.” The reading I would defend is the one requiring no filter at all: money growing 5.3–6.8% over four quarters against a 4.25–5.0% speed limit, i.e. modestly above sustainable, with all aggregates agreeing.

After this paper was first posted, the 2026Q2 national accounts were released. The real-side nowcast proved nearly exact but the GDP deflator came in at 6.09% against an assumed 3.24%, moving every gap estimate down by up to 1.2 percentage points and eliminating the only two specifications whose bands had excluded zero. A single quarter of data and a routine vendor revision were sufficient to reverse the one qualitative claim the estimates supported — an unplanned demonstration of the paper's own argument, documented in Section 8.1.

title: LGBT+ Rights and Democracy in the United States

detail.title: LGBT+ Rights and Democracy in the United States
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the features of liberal democracy in the United States' first 250 years that have been most conducive to LGBT+ freedom are those which are least related to the archetypical form of democracy: majority rule. It is federalism, common law Constitutionalism, the rule of law, and First Amendment rights that have contributed most to the promotion of LGBT+ rights. The ideal of "government by discussion" stands out as the ideal by which LGBT+ freedoms have been won through a tumultuous process. Thus, LGBT+ inclusion is a triumph of liberalism, not democracy. The discussion then examines future directions and challenges for achieving and maintaining LGBT+ freedom.

title: Pricing the Invisible Borrower: An Actuarial Approach to the Design of Dynamic Credit Extension

detail.title: Pricing the Invisible Borrower: An Actuarial Approach to the Design of Dynamic Credit Extension
detail.abstract: At least 1.3 billion people worldwide hold no credit score and no financial transaction history. Existing lending institutions have kept this population structurally excluded (Diamond, 1989; Pagano and Jappelli, 1993), and real-world lending practice turns out, on inspection, to rely on a coarse rule of thumb rather than a theoretically optimized policy: this study's analysis of real data from Home Credit Group (more than 210,000 loans, 13.6 million repayment records, and 3.84 million monthly card balances) makes this concrete. This paper proposes a combination not previously found in the literature: applying actuarial credibility theory (Buhlmann, 1967; Buhlmann and Straub, 1970) to the design of dynamic credit expansion. A hierarchical Bayesian model, written θ(n, q), decomposes borrower risk into a structural floor and an individual component that shrinks with observed history. The model is derived along two independent routes, a linear least-squares credibility argument and the exact Bayes posterior mean (Jewell, 1974), and is calibrated against real data with R 2 = 0.87 and 0.84. This θ(n, q) is then integrated into a single framework spanning contract theory, behavioral economics, dynamic programming, and multi-lender equilibrium analysis, producing an implementable closed-form credit limit function L * (n, q). The Monte Carlo validation does not deliver the result originally hoped for, namely that theory beats practice outright; instead the finding is reframed as a normative benchmark, a ruler against which the lending rules used in practice can be measured. This honest course correction is itself part of the paper's methodological contribution.

title: The Economics of AI Capital under Limited Observability: Relational Frontiers, the Capital Stack, and a Research Program

detail.title: The Economics of AI Capital under Limited Observability: Relational Frontiers, the Capital Stack, and a Research Program
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence can qualify as economic capital under the classical definition—a durable stock yielding a service flow—but modeled governance may require observation of specified assertions. Observation alone is insufficient; valuation may require market, cost, service-flow, rights, and risk evidence. The framework distinguishes productive activity, productive configuration, and institutional claim formation. Activity may occur unobserved. People, AI, data, rights, authority, and operating conditions may form a productive configuration before an institution defines its boundaries, supplies sufficient evidence and governance responsibility, and admits it to a governed capital inventory. The record does not create the activity or configuration; it individuates the institution’s governance-and-valuation claim by specifying components, boundaries, capabilities, authority, and evidence. Admission denotes this claim-formation event; admitted describes the bounded, evidenced configuration after acquiring institutional status. An operating AI deployment is therefore not necessarily the admitted synthetic-capital object defined here. Modeled admission neither causes nor determines accounting recognition, capitalization, deferral, presentation, or disclosure. The paper models deployed AI capital as a typed object indexed by capital-stack position and relational-frontier family. Under §6’s protected-floor and local-domain assumptions, no continuous scalar summary can remain sensitive to positive substitutable gains while ranking every floor-satisfying bundle above every floor-violating bundle. Under §7’s backward-looking convention, positive drift, and unrestricted local-diffusion approximation away from the nonnegative boundary, fixed-cadence reporting produces expected signed understatement. Neither derivation has been independently certified. An operator’s decision problem includes a positive outside option for unadmitted operation. Three conditional results follow: attestation spending below a positive admission threshold is dominated by zero spending when sub-threshold evidence has no benefit; a sufficiently short expected life can make the admission premium inadequate to recover a positive crossing cost; and, when irreducible dependency prevents admission at every investment level, zero attestation investment is optimal even if deployment continues. These results require the stated outside-option, concavity, interior-crossing, reachability, life, and tie-breaking conditions. Operational attestation means model-defined evidence collection, evaluation, and recording, not—unless stated—a professional attestation engagement or independent practitioner’s conclusion. Four metrics follow. The AI-expenditure capitalization rate is the regime-specific share of AI-attributed eligible costs in a declared population that accounting rules require to be capitalized, including zero. It neither implies recognition of the composite object as a distinct accounting category nor measures governed admission, value creation, or capital formation. The self-observation deficit is the question- and universe-specific share of eligible organizations unable to report the requested aspect of AI use. Evidence age is the conditional median age of qualifying capability records; organizations lacking such records are reported separately. Capability-to-governance lag is a censored time-to-first-governed-deployment distribution whose median is reported only when identified. The metrics differ in units, populations, weighting, missingness, and aggregation. Appendix B treats links to accounting, reporting, and assurance as a jurisdiction-bounded research agenda rather than interchangeable systems. A governed-admission rate is the closer firm-level counterpart to the theory. Procurement form can alter the cost mix and capitalized share; lower integration may separately reduce governed admission. Adoption, capitalization, and governed admission may diverge, but none identifies the others’ mechanism without component-level and admission data. Six propositions, specified only after public release, are compared with United Kingdom aggregate data not designed or collected by the author. For Proposition 1, the aggregates show only a descriptive breadth-versus-depth pattern and lack the held-out outcome data needed to test whether a preregistered, typed deployment measure adds out-of-sample predictive or decision value beyond adoption alone. Three other propositions have suggestive proxies but are not established; two cannot be evaluated; none is confirmed.

title: Plan Coordination, LGBT+ Identities, and The Extent of the Market

detail.title: Plan Coordination, LGBT+ Identities, and The Extent of the Market
detail.abstract: Markets set LGBT+ individuals free and promote their wellbeing in a way that other forms of social coordination do not. Societies have three broad means of preventing conflict and upheaval of members' plans. These include relying on evolved norms, delegating plan-making to a single entity, and negotiating between delimited spheres of decision making. These have been labeled, respectively, Tradition, Planning, and the Market. Traditional norms have not produced significant increases in living standards and have constrained some groups, such as LGBT+ individuals, to stifling social roles. Planning likewise fails to enable the kind of experimentation that facilitates LGBT+ freedom. Market-based societies, however, have seen significant advances in the flourishing of such individuals. On the extensive margin, more activities coordinated by explicit negotiation in a market or market-like setting permits greater flexibility in the life plans these individuals can execute. On the intensive margin, the extent of the market permits specialization in ways that improve the fit between LGBT+ individuals' distinct preferences and the goods available to them.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Partial Homogeneity in Staggered Difference-in-Difference
affiliations: Ashoka University - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Bayesian Approach to Partial Homogeneity in Staggered Difference-in-Difference
detail.abstract: In staggered difference-indifferences (DiD) designs, units enter treatment at different calendar times, so the treatment effect is not a single number but a set of Cohort-Average Treatment effects on the Treated (CATTs), one per cohort-time cell. Estimating every CATT as its own parameter, as the standard fully flexible estimator does, is unbiased but inefficient when some of these effects are in fact equal, whereas pooling them all into a single two-way fixed effects (TWFE) coefficient is efficient but biased whenever the heterogeneity is genuine. We frame the choice between these extremes as a partition-selection problem on the cohort-time cells and address it with a Dirichlet Process (DP) mixture prior on the CATTs. The model favors parsimonious groupings without fixing their number, and a collapsed Gibbs sampler delivers point estimates, credible intervals that marginalize the unknown partition, and co-clustering probabilities for every pair of CATTs. With the error variance held fixed, the model's maximum a posteriori (MAP) partition reduces to an ℓ 0-penalized regression, connecting the Bayesian formulation to the homogeneity-pursuit literature. In a calibrated simulation, the model cuts the sampling variance of the cohort-time effects by 26-52% relative to the fully flexible estimator, without the pooled estimator's bias, provided the distinct effects are separated enough to be recovered, and the posterior delivers near-nominal confidence-interval coverage by averaging over the unknown partition. In two applications the method recovers a precision-improving partial-homogeneity structure in one, where the cohort-time effects are genuinely heterogeneous, and reports that full pooling is adequate in the other, where they are not.

title: Multiple Equilibria and the Phillips Curve: Do Agents Always Underreact?
affiliations: Ca’ Foscari University of Venice, University Ca' Foscari of Venice - Department of Economics and Università Ca' Foscari Venezia

detail.title: Multiple Equilibria and the Phillips Curve: Do Agents Always Underreact?
detail.abstract: Many specifications of the New Keynesian Phillips curve (NKPC) assume that agents forecast inflation using a simple, potentially misspecified rule. The consistency conditions linking the perceived and actual laws of motion may generate multiple expectation consistent equilibria, making the mapping from structural parameters to observables non unique and complicating likelihood-based inference. We address this problem by introducing a latent Markov-switching process that links equilibrium specific reduced form parameterizations to statistical regimes. A Bayesian framework with hierarchical priors allows us to assess whether the estimated regimes conform to the theoretical equilibrium restrictions and to measure their posterior relevance over time. Using U.S. inflation, the output gap, and consensus expectations from the Survey of Professional Forecasters, we find evidence of multiple, well separated regimes associated with different levels of perceived inflation persistence. Forecast errors display systematic underreaction in the high-persistence regimes, whereas responses in the low-persistence regime are not systematically different from the full information benchmark. The model reproduces inflation dynamics during the Great Recession without generating the large disinflation predicted by some conventional NKPC specifications.

title: Information Capital and Career Lock-In
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Information Capital and Career Lock-In
detail.abstract: I examine the problem of a risk-averse agent who faces uncertainty about his ability in a particular task, or career. Ability can only be measured, up to Gaussian noise, by observing output. The agent has access to an “experimentation” technology—a durable, career-specific stock built by costly investment—that raises the precision with which output reveals ability, and he may pay a fixed cost to abandon the career and draw a new one. Although beliefs evolve without bound in precision, I show that in posterior-variance form the problem is a stationary dynamic program on a compact belief state, with the known-ability model as its boundary. The optimal policy is a reservation posterior mean that is decreasing in the accumulated experimentation stock: information capital is lost upon switching, so experienced experimenters tolerate worse news before quitting—an information-capital lock-in effect. Near the switching boundary, the value function is locally increasing in belief uncertainty: the real-option value of learning outweighs the risk premium that uncertainty commands under risk aversion. Simulated careers display front-loaded experimentation, rapid abandonment of bad draws, and decay of learning effort with tenure.

title: Screening with Concealable Capabilities: Virtual Values beyond Ordered Types *
affiliations: Hangzhou Dianzi University and

detail.title: Screening with Concealable Capabilities: Virtual Values beyond Ordered Types *

detail.abstract: In many contracting problems the agent's private information is a portfolio of capabilities: it can be demonstrated and understated, and it cannot be fabricated, so portfolios are ranked by inclusion, a partial order. We develop the theory of profit-maximizing mechanisms with transfers for such environments, where a type's information rent is the largest gain along any descending chain of impersonations. The classical screening package survives exactly on order structures in which every type has a unique impersonation route ("downward forests"): there, trade is governed by a poset virtual surplus built from cost increments and upper-set masses, ironing is optimization over the vertices of the order polytope, and optimal mechanisms are deterministic. Beyond forests, competing routes take over: the optimum randomizes for generic costs on an open set of priors, shaving one incomparable type's trade to equalize another type's impersonation options, and, with competing agents, Bayesian design strictly outperforms dominant strategies. Route competition has two independent sources, width in the order and heterogeneity across actions, and either one alone breaks both deterministic optimality and dominant-strategy equivalence; the failures are certified in exact arithmetic. Incomparability itself benefits the principal: payoff-matched deletions of comparabilities raise revenue, up to full extraction on antichains, making the architecture of capabilities a screening instrument.

title: Development Assistance for Health and Domestic Spending, 1990–2050: An Up-to-Date Assessment of the 2025 Aid Cuts
affiliations: University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington - Department of Health Metrics Sciences, University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation and University of Washington - Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation

detail.title: Development Assistance for Health and Domestic Spending, 1990–2050: An Up-to-Date Assessment of the 2025 Aid Cuts

detail.abstract:
Background: In 2024 and 2025, several major bilateral donors including the USA, the UK, Germany, and France announced cuts to official development assistance. Recipient countries have had varied responses to these cuts. This instability makes a systematic and comprehensive tracking of the flow of health resources more essential for stakeholders than ever before. To provide this information, this study uses the latest available data to provide updated synopsis of the cuts in development assistance for health (DAH), initial government responses, and changes in total health spending in context.   

Methods: We generated estimates for all four sources of health financing, including DAH, government spending, prepaid private, and out-of-pocket (OOP) health spending from 1990 through the present and then forecasted those estimates through 2050. The latest spending and budget reports were used for WHO, the World Bank, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), ministries of health and finance websites, and all major providers of DAH. Where applicable, we used ensemble and spatiotemporal Gaussian modelling techniques to generate estimates. We report uncertainty intervals.    

Findings: DAH peaked in 2021 at $81·3 billion and decreased to $44·9 billion in 2025 and $42·5 billion in 2026. In aggregate, the fraction that has been committed to countries has dropped by 3·6 percentage points, although for the US the drop is 18·6 points. Government spending per person ranged from $2·16 to $8519 in 2025. While government allocation to the health sector has increased in several countries, increases in low-income countries are not generally in the order of magnitude that fully covers the gap.  Lastly, long-term forecasts of health spending point to a widening in the gap in per person spending globally. 

Interpretation: Reductions in aid have been a notable disruption in the global health financing architecture. The large reductions in aggregate mask the even more disruptive effects at the country level as early observation suggests that many funds remain unallocated in 2025 and 2026. A proactive effort from national governments to access the internal fiscal capacity to cover the gap comprehensively is needed to ensure that gaps in service provision are filled on time and population health outcomes are preserved in the long term.

title: Aggregate Perceived Risk -A Unified Asset Pricing Framework

detail.title: Aggregate Perceived Risk -A Unified Asset Pricing Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of dQuant Capital Management, an investment firm that utilizes quantitative strategies. The theoretical framework presented in this paper, including the Aggregate Perceived Risk (APR) model, informs the proprietary methodologies used by the firm. No external funding was received for this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Yes, make my paper Publicly Available.

detail.abstract: The Aggregate Perceived Risk (APR) framework provides a unified asset-pricing architecture that reconciles neoclassical valuation, behavioral dynamics, and market microstructure within a single non-linear equation (P t = V t /(APR t) k). By endogenizing volatility clustering, regime shifts, and heavy tails, the model bridges orderly equilibria and tail-risk dislocations without exogenous shocks. APR delivers five core results: (1) a unified non-linear operator with state-dependent fundamental transmission; (2) a derivative-based alpha protocol identifying non-linear inflection points; (3) proof that endogenous jumps stem from denominator-exponent perception dynamics; (4) a resolution to the Parameter Paradox, where structural tightening becomes expansionary (∂P t /∂k > 0) in hyper-complacent regimes; and (5) a microstructural mechanism for continuous-time bubbles and crashes. Ultimately, APR establishes a unified mathematical foundation for price formation across normal and crisis regimes.

title: Flights of the Living Dead: Zombie Credit and Product Market Competition
affiliations: Alliance Manchester Business School and University of Virginia - McIntire School

detail.title: Flights of the Living Dead: Zombie Credit and Product Market Competition
detail.abstract: We use granular US airline data to study price and non-price competition between "zombies"-nonviable firms sustained by subsidized lending-and their healthy, bankrupt, and non-subsidizeddistressed rivals in well-defined product markets. While we confirm that markets with zombies exhibit fare disinflation, we show that this result is mostly driven by the non-zombie carriers, especially the non-subsidized distressed. A Bartik-style shift-share instrument supports a causal interpretation. Consistent with strategic responses to zombie pressure, the non-subsidized distressed carriers also cut fares preemptively in markets threatened by zombie entry, and they improve their service quality in markets in which they directly compete with zombies. Yet, the aggressive competition does not pay off: The non-zombie carriers lose market share and are more likely to exit relative to their less efficient zombies rivals. Zombie lending thus distorts both competitive behavior and market selection.

title: Multidimensional Physical Fitness Subtypes and Year-To-Year State Transitions among University Students in Eastern China: A Longitudinal Cohort Study of 316,609 Students from More Than 150 Institutions
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Southeast University, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Southeast University, Yunnan University, Southeast University, The University of Sydney and Beijing Sport University

detail.title: Multidimensional Physical Fitness Subtypes and Year-To-Year State Transitions among University Students in Eastern China: A Longitudinal Cohort Study of 316,609 Students from More Than 150 Institutions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Zhongda Hospital, Southeast University (approval number 2026ZDKYSB0417). All included participants provided written informed consent.

detail.abstract:
Background: Whether multidimensional developmental subtypes of physical fitness exist among university students, and how these states change across four years of university, remains unclear.

Methods: We used longitudinal data from the National Student Physical Health Standard Test in an eastern province of China, covering all higher education institutions in the province. The analytic sample included 316,609 students (159,944 men and 156,665 women), each with complete physical fitness records for four academic years. Height-adjusted vital capacity, BMI, standing long jump, 50-m sprint, 800/1000-m run, and sit-ups in women were entered into Gaussian finite mixture models to identify integrated physical fitness subtypes. Year-to-year state transitions were characterised using mixture models fitted independently within each academic year.

Findings: Five integrated physical fitness subtypes were identified in men and six in women. Baseline BMI was the strongest predictor of membership in adverse subtypes (odds ratio for the high-BMI endurance-decline subtype vs the lean overall-optimal subtype in men, 6.16 [95% CI 6.01–6.31]), whereas height-adjusted vital capacity had almost no independent predictive value (OR 1.00 [0.97–1.02]). Students who spent their entire first academic year under COVID-19 restrictions in the 2020 entry cohort did not have a higher prevalence of adverse subtypes than those in the 2021 cohort (men: 12.7% vs 13.9%). Year-to-year persistence in the poorest fitness state (S6) was consistently lower than persistence in the best state (S1; men, S6: 3.4%–35.0% vs S1: 51.4%–65.1%). In women, only 37.2% of those in S1 in the first year remained in S1 in the second year.

Interpretation: The identification of robust multidimensional physical fitness subtypes in a province-wide population, together with the finding that BMI and sprint performance outperformed vital capacity for risk stratification, suggests that resource-efficient screening strategies could be implemented across different types of higher education institutions in the Western Pacific region. The high mobility at the lower end of the fitness distribution and the instability of the optimal first-year state among women indicate that physical fitness surveillance in young adults should be based on developmentally timed repeated screening rather than one-off classification.

title: The Impact of Bogotá’s Primary Health Care Oriented Reorganisation on Clinical and Economic Outcomes in Adults with Hypertension: Quasi-Experimental Analysis ​
affiliations: National University of Colombia, Imperial College London, Imperial College London - Public Health Policy Evaluation Unit and National University of Colombia

detail.title: The Impact of Bogotá’s Primary Health Care Oriented Reorganisation on Clinical and Economic Outcomes in Adults with Hypertension: Quasi-Experimental Analysis ​

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was obtained from the Faculty of Medicine Ethics Committee at Universidad Nacional de Colombia (approval letter B.FM.1.002 -CE-0063 -23), and data was accessed on March 16th, 2024.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the NIHR (NIHR150067) using UK international development funding from the UK Government to support global health research. TH and CM are supported by the NIHR (grant number NIHR133252).

detail.abstract:
Introduction: In 2016, Bogotá reorganised its public health-care network into four integrated service delivery subnetworks, expanded Priority Health Care Centres, reduced administrative barriers, and introduced payment mechanisms linked to continuity and quality. We assessed the effects of this reform on clinical outcomes, health-care use, and direct health-care costs among adults with hypertension. 

Methods: We conducted a quasi-experimental analysis using a propensity score-matched difference-in-differences approach and administrative data from adults with hypertension between 2015 and 2018. We compared outcomes aggregated in fixed six-month observation intervals among individuals insured under the subsidised scheme, who were exposed to the public-sector reorganisation, with individuals insured under the contributory scheme, who were not directly exposed. Outcomes, measured in fixed 6-month intervals, were outpatient visits, all-cause hospital admissions, myocardial revascularisation, dialysis, direct health-care costs, and all-cause mortality. Linear fixed-effects models estimated effects for continuous outcomes, and logistic models were used for mortality. 

Results: The eligible cohort included 443,344 adults aged 18 ≥ years with hypertension before matching (38,027 subsidised; 405,317 contributory). The reform was associated with increased outpatient utilisation (Average Treatment Effect (ATE)=0.05 visits per patient per semester, defined as a fixed six-month observation interval; 95% CI 0.04–0.06). All-cause hospitalisations among patients with hypertension decreased (ATE=–0.002; 95% CI –0.002 to –0.001), representing roughly one fewer admission per 500 patients per semester. Healthcare costs declined substantially (ATE=–1.02; 95% CI –1.23 to –0.80), and mortality decreased, with a 13% reduction in the odds of death in the subsidised population following the reform (Odds Ratio=0.87; 95% CI 0.79–0.95). Robustness analyses showed consistent results across specifications. 

Conclusion: Bogotá’s public-sector reorganisation was associated with increased outpatient care and reductions in hospital admissions, direct costs, and mortality among adults with hypertension in the subsidised scheme. Integrated public-sector delivery reforms could improve chronic disease outcomes in fragmented health systems

title: Clinical Efficacy and Safety of Microwave Ablation versus Repeat Surgery for New or Progressive Pulmonary Nodules in Patients with a History of Lung Resection: A Propensity Score Weighted Analysis
affiliations: Nanjing Medical University, Nanjing Medical University, Nanjing University and Nanjing University

detail.title: Clinical Efficacy and Safety of Microwave Ablation versus Repeat Surgery for New or Progressive Pulmonary Nodules in Patients with a History of Lung Resection: A Propensity Score Weighted Analysis
