detail.abstract:
Background: The increasing detection of multiple primary lung cancers (MPLC) and residual nodule progression in patients with a history of lung resection poses a significant clinical dilemma. These patients often have diminished pulmonary reserve or are averse to repeat thoracotomy, rendering a second surgery challenging. This study aimed to compare the clinical efficacy and safety of computed tomography (CT)-guided percutaneous microwave ablation (MWA) versus repeat surgical resection for new or progressive pulmonary nodules in this specific population.

Methods: This single-center retrospective case-control study included patients with a history of lung resection for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who subsequently developed new or progressive nodules requiring intervention. Patients were divided into the MWA group and the repeat surgery group. The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), and secondary outcomes included progression-free survi:val (PFS), length of hospital stay, duration of postoperative analgesic use, and complications. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was employed to adjust for potential confounding variables.

Findings: A total of 50 patients were included (MWA, n=21; surgery, n=29). After IPTW adjustment, baseline characteristics were well-balanced between groups. MWA was associated with significantly shorter hospital stays (weighted median: 2 vs. 4 days, P=0.003) and reduced duration of analgesic use (weighted median: 0 vs. 4 days, P<0.001). The incidence of pleural effusion was significantly lower in the MWA group (0% vs. 20%, P=0.013). No significant differences were observed in PFS between the two groups (weighted log-rank P=0.55), and no deaths occurred during follow-up, precluding formal OS comparison.

Interpretation: For strictly selected patients with a history of lung resection and new or progressive subsolid nodules, MWA offers comparable short-to-medium-term PFS to repeat surgery while providing significant perioperative advantages, including shorter hospitalization, less postoperative pain, and fewer complications. MWA should be considered a viable alternative in the multidisciplinary team (MDT) decision-making process for these challenging cases.

title: A Theory of Finance: Allocation, Primitives, and Informational Distance

detail.title: A Theory of Finance: Allocation, Primitives, and Informational Distance
detail.abstract:
Modern financial theory largely begins with risk. It asks how measurable exposure should be allocated, diversified, transferred, and priced. This paper argues that such analysis begins after a prior financial problem has already been addressed. Financial commitments must become sufficiently knowable, verifiable, and enforceable before their uncertainty can be represented as risk. 

The paper therefore treats uncertainty as the more primitive obstacle to financial allocation and separates it into information-independent uncertainty and uncertainty arising from informational distance. The first reflects the openness of the future. The second arises from separation between a financial commitment and the information required to identify, evaluate, and respond to the conditions on which it depends. 

This distinction changes the object and order of financial optimization. Financial architecture first reduces informational-distance uncertainty where doing so is feasible and economically justified. The remaining uncertainty can then be represented as risk, redistributed through diversification, insurance, and financial engineering, and priced through financial markets. 

The framework interprets finance as performing three related functions: reducing informational distance, redistributing residual uncertainty, and pricing the exposure that remains. It also provides a common basis for evaluating financial institutions, innovation, firm behavior, professional practice, and regulation. Modern finance remains essential, but it becomes a conditional theory operating within an informational environment that finance itself can partly change.

title: Venture Capital and Government Policy *
affiliations: Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Space Engineering University, University of Wisconsin-Madison,  and Government of Canada - Bank of Canada

detail.title: Venture Capital and Government Policy *
detail.abstract: This paper studies venture capital using search theory. Different from past work, we include public and private VCs (venture capitalists), capturing the fact that governments are actively involved in some VC markets, like China, where public exceeds private investment. We analyze how public policies affect private participation, time on the market, payoffs, etc. Theory predicts that for some parameters public VCs crowd in, not out, private VCs. Empirical findings are consistent with this prediction: In Chinese data, government VC investment increases private investment in a location-industry area, and promotes entry of firms in the area and along their supply chain.

title: When Personalization Becomes Bias: Structural and Discursive Religious Framing in AI-Generated Financial Advice
affiliations: Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) - College of Liberal Arts, Hitotsubashi University,  and Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) - Saunders College of Business

detail.title: When Personalization Becomes Bias: Structural and Discursive Religious Framing in AI-Generated Financial Advice
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated in financial advisory systems, yet their role in reproducing religious bias remains underexamined. This study provides systematic mixed-methods evidence of such bias across three LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok) using 432 simulated advisorclient interactions spanning 16 religious identity pairings (Christian, Muslim, Hindu, and non-religious baseline) and three core household financial decisions: stock investment, house purchase, and life insurance. Combining regression and reflexive thematic analyses, we identify structural biases across models and decision contexts, and discursive mechanisms through which these biases are linguistically enacted. Quantitative results show that unbiased advice appeared in only 12-18% of cases, with Gemini consistently producing higher bias than Grok, while ChatGPT's outputs were statistically comparable to Grok's. Religiously symmetric advisor-client pairings almost always triggered explicit religious framing, and even non-religious clients often received advisor-centered religious appeals. Qualitative findings reveal that bias is linguistically manifested through religious anchoring, uneven cultural signaling, and tone modulation, varying systematically by model and financial scenario. Stock investment prompts produced higher financially technical responses, whereas life insurance advice triggered stronger religious language. The study develops a dual-dimensional framework linking structural bias rooted in model training and design with discursive bias expressed through language, advancing understanding of algorithmic bias in LLM-generated financial advice. It also demonstrates that such advice adapts linguistically to identity cues, revealing a broader managerial dilemma between personalization and neutrality. Finally, the study highlights managerial implications for businesses, financial institutions, and regulators seeking to ensure neutrality, cultural sensitivity, and trust in AI-mediated advice.

title: Oil-Krone Divergence and OSEAX Returns Across Regimes

detail.title: Oil-Krone Divergence and OSEAX Returns Across Regimes

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether short-term disagreements between crude oil price movements and the Norwegian krone exchange rate carry predictive information for next-day returns on the Oslo Stock Exchange (OSEAX), and whether any such predictability depends on the prevailing market regime. Motivated by Driesprong et al. (2003), who documented a gradualdiffusion underreaction effect of oil prices on equity returns, this project constructs an original divergence signal from the standardized returns of Brent crude and the USD/NOK exchange rate, and a regime classifier based on the rolling correlation between the All-Share index and oil, using daily data from 2016 to 2025. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, the signal has no predictive power in the petro regime (𝑡 = −0.70) but is statistically significant in the decoupled regime (𝑡 = 3.66, 𝑝 = 0.0003). The effect proves robust to the smoothing window and regime threshold and, most demandingly, to time. It remains significant in both the 2016–2021 and 2021–2025 subsamples, splitting almost exactly as a temporally uniform effect predicts. The explained variance is nonetheless economically modest (𝑅 2 ≈ 1.14%), consistent with the broader literature on the modesty of return-predictability signals in liquid markets. Converted into a trading rule, the signal yields a directional edge of comparable size, but a strategy built on it earns less than simply holding the index; its value lies in diversification rather than outperformance, with a market beta near zero and roughly half the index's volatility. Blending the strategy with the index confirms this directly: a 70/30 market/strategy portfolio returns 12.34% annually at 11.75% volatility (Sharpe 1.05), a 50/50 blend returns 11.67% at 9.21% volatility (Sharpe 1.27) and a 30/70 blend returns 10.83% at just 8.00% volatility (Sharpe 1.35) — all improving on the index alone, which returns 12.99 per cent at 16.69 per cent volatility for a Sharpe of 0.78. Conditioning the strategy on signal strength or depth of decoupling does not improve it. The contribution is therefore a signal that is statistically robust, economically small, and structurally rather than episodically motivated.

title: Antitrust Analysis in Tipped Markets
affiliations: University of Utah - College of Social & Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Antitrust Analysis in Tipped Markets
detail.abstract: High-technology platform markets have a well-known tendency to tip towards a single dominant firm. "Tipped markets"-cases where this tipping process has already played out and the dominant firm is entrenched by network effects, switching costs, and/or vertical integration-raise novel antitrust concerns. Application of standard tools in such markets can lead to misleading results for several reasons. First, a dominant platform might rationally never maximize short-run profits. Second, market definition and competitive-effects analysis are often inseparable because the challenged conduct has shaped the market's structure from inception. Third, exclusionary conduct may distort observed diversion by weakening the rivals that would otherwise be the closest substitutes. Finally, because tipped markets often lack a competitive benchmark, the Consumer Welfare Standard can impose an evidentiary burden that is difficult or impossible for plaintiffs to satisfy. The Protect Competition Standard could offer some advantages in these settings by focusing on whether conduct impairs rivals' opportunities and incentives to compete, rather than requiring speculative proof of but-for outcomes.

title: The Digital Vulnerability Paradox: Who Really Falls for Disinformation in Europe?
affiliations: ,  and University of Almería

detail.title: The Digital Vulnerability Paradox: Who Really Falls for Disinformation in Europe?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: European governments are increasingly restricting minors’ access to social media on the assumption that young people are uniquely vulnerable to disinformation. This article tests that assumption empirically. Drawing on the Flash Eurobarometer 3592 (Social Media Survey 2025), a representative sample of 26,121 citizens across the 27 EU member states, we examine how age relates to self-perceived confidence in detecting disinformation and to actual verification behaviour, measured through a proactive verification index. The results reveal a vulnerability paradox: the 15–24 cohort targeted by age-restriction policies reports the lowest subjective confidence yet performs the most proactive verification, while adults aged 55 and over are more than three times as likely to verify nothing at all. Interaction models show that overconfidence suppresses verification most strongly among older cohorts. Because young Europeans also rely most heavily on platforms for civic information, blanket age restrictions risk informational disenfranchisement. We argue for a shift from exclusionary protectionism towards architectural empowerment through verification-by-design.

title: A Study of Structured Products Awareness and Investment Preferences.

detail.title: A Study of Structured Products Awareness and Investment Preferences.
detail.abstract: The study aims at analyzing the “Structured products awareness and investment preferences”, how much they have evolved in these past five years and what are its future aspects. This study will be relevant for the Investors and the Brokers to understand about the new emerging concept Structured products and help them in taking informed decisions.

title: Black Strikebreakers, Industrial Opportunity, and Racial Inequality
affiliations: Bowdoin College and Marquette University

detail.title: Black Strikebreakers, Industrial Opportunity, and Racial Inequality
detail.abstract: During the late-nineteenth and early-twentieth centuries, Black Americans faced many employment restrictions, including exclusion from industrial work, leading some to engage in the contentious act of strikebreaking. Although Black strikebreaking is well documented in history, its long-run economic effects remain poorly understood. This paper examines whether strikebreaking enabled Black workers to break industrial employment barriers and reduce racial inequality. Using data on the county, year, and industry of Black strikebreaker use, we find that strikebreaking increased the Black share of employment by about 2 percentage points in affected county-industry pairs — an effect that persisted for up to 40 years. We also find evidence that the Black–White wage gap in 1940 was roughly 8 log points smaller in affected pairs. We provide suggestive evidence that the lasting impact of Black strikebreakers on Black labor shares reflects persistent changes in employers' hiring practices, while the narrowing of the wage gap reflects gains in Black unionization in affected industries.

title: Generalizing Intensive Care AI across Time Scales in Resource-Limited Settings
affiliations: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi, Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Bhopal, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) - Department of Pediatrics and Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology - Guru Angad Dev Veterinary and Animal Science University, Ludhiana (Punjab),

detail.title: Generalizing Intensive Care AI across Time Scales in Resource-Limited Settings

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of AIIMS, New Delhi (approval numbers IEC/NP-211/08·05·2015 and IEC-787/07.10.2022, RP-14/2022). The requirement for individual informed consent was waived because the study involved retrospective analysis of routinely collected clinical data, and all data were anonymized before use.
declarations.funderStatement: This research work was supported by the SafeICU Initiative, funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) under grant award number A1-Ad-hoc/18/2022-A1-Cell; the Centre of Excellence in Healthcare (COEH) at IIIT-Delhi; and Wellcome Trust/DBT India Alliance Fellowship (IA/CPHE/14/1/501504) awarded to Prof Tavpritesh Sethi.

detail.abstract:
Generalization remains a major barrier to the clinical deployment of artificial intelligence in critical care. Models developed using high-frequency physiological monitoring often experience performance degradation when applied across hospitals, patient populations, and monitoring environments that differ from those used during training. Although variability in temporal resolution is widespread in critical care, its impact on representation learning and model transferability remains poorly understood.Here,  we introduce the resolution-transfer task for physiological time series and present PhysioStack, a self-supervised physiological representation learning framework designed to evaluate whether representations learned from high-frequency monitoring data remain robust across clinically relevant monitoring frequencies without retraining. We introduce SafeICU, a longitudinal pediatric intensive care dataset spanning ten years of routinely collected clinical and physiological data from a tertiary-care hospital in India, including high-resolution vital signs recorded at 15-second intervals. Transformer-based masked language models were trained on 144,271 patient-hours of high-resolution physiological signals from 984 pediatric ICU stays to learn representations of heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and arterial blood pressure. 

Representations learned at high temporal resolution demonstrated strong transferability across lower monitoring frequencies, consistently outperforming models trained directly on temporally aggregated data. Importantly, these representations generalized across patient populations, maintaining performance when evaluated on independent adult intensive care cohorts derived from the MIMIC-III and eICU databases without retraining. In a downstream early shock prediction task, PhysioStack achieved AUROC values of 0.82-0.86 and AUPRC values of 0.91-0.94 across 5-60‑minute monitoring frequencies without retraining. Representations trained on pediatric data generalized to independent adult ICU cohorts, achieving AUROC 0.91-0.95 and AUPRC 0.94-0.97 without cohort-specific fine-tuning.

These findings demonstrate that PhysioStack learns transferable physiological representations that generalize across temporal resolutions and patient cohorts, supporting robust AI for critical care. To support further research, we publicly release the SafeICU database, comprising longitudinal vital signs, laboratory measurements, treatment records, microbiology, and admission and discharge, together with pretrained physiological representation models.

title: Linking Customers to Firm-managed Assets: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment on Symbolic Adoption
affiliations: Cornell University - Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management, Johns Hopkins University and

detail.title: Linking Customers to Firm-managed Assets: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment on Symbolic Adoption
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Many service firms attract customers and deliver experiences through firm-managed physical assets, such as plants in botanical gardens, animals in aquariums, and artworks in museums. Yet customers typically encounter these assets only as part of a broader service experience, without forming an ongoing connection to a particular asset. We examine whether symbolic adoption, an emerging service practice that links customers to existing service assets while firms retain ownership and operational responsibility, can increase customer demand. Methodology/results: We conduct a randomized field experiment in collaboration with an ecological park. The sample includes 533 prior customers who voluntarily registered for a symbolic adoption program. We randomly assigned 266 applicants to receive the program and 267 to a control condition. Treated customers were linked to specific strawberry-plant units, whereas control customers did not receive access. Using a difference-in-differences analysis of weekly customer-level data, we estimate the effect of receiving the program relative to not receiving it among registered applicants. Assignment to the program increases weekly visits by 0.1242 visits per customer-week and log weekly spending by 0.1437 during active implementation. The spending effects extend beyond the asset-linked category: assignment to the program increases spending on strawberries and other product categories. These effects persist during the observed six-week post-program period after the active program and its associated touchpoints ended. Managerial implications: Symbolic adoption can increase repeat visits and broaden on-site demand by linking customers to existing firm-managed assets. Firms can use this approach to engage customers and increase on-site spending without substantial investment in new physical assets, while retaining ownership and operational responsibility. An accounting analysis further suggests potential positive net value under the stated assumptions.

title: Market Architecture and Exogenous State Transitions: Evidence from Climate Regimes in Commodity Markets

detail.title: Market Architecture and Exogenous State Transitions: Evidence from Climate Regimes in Commodity Markets
detail.abstract: Do exogenous climate regimes reorganize the dependence structure of commodity markets, or do they merely shift the general level of co-movement? We introduce the concept of Market Architecture-defined as the persistent topological organization of long-run dependence, invariant to common shifts in the level of correlation-and develop an estimable Block Factor DCC-MIDAS model whose long-run correlation target is analytic and positive definite. Using twenty commodity futures spanning five sectors from November 2, 2000 to June 29, 2026 (T = 6,469), and ENSO states as an exogenous indexing device, we find that El Nino and La Nina operate through two distinct channels. La Nina raises system-wide average long-run correlation by 9.5 percentage points, constituting a system-wide integration shock. After removing this level effect, El Nino is associated with differentiated architecture: Grains and Metals tighten relative to the system mean while Energy and Livestock remain flat, reorganizing the relative structure of dependence across sectors. The evidence supports the theoretical distinction between level and topology proposed in the paper's foundational propositions. A three-factor specification is selected by BIC (ΔBIC =-833.3) and confirmed by nine independent starts. The results document a predictive association between climate regimes and market architecture, with implications for regime-conditional risk management.

reference: FRB of Cleveland Working Paper No. 26-19; https://doi.org/10.26509/frbc-wp-202619
title: Financial and Production Integration in the Macroeconomy
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome, , Michigan State University and Michigan State University

detail.title: Financial and Production Integration in the Macroeconomy

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Cleveland Working Paper No. 26-19
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies how integration between the financial sector and production networks shapes business cycle transmission. We develop a dynamic model in which banks provide asset-based financing to firms embedded in supply chains. The model highlights two margins of bank–supply chain integration with opposite macroeconomic implications. Extensive-margin integration—captured by firms' access to banks specializing in different supply chain segments—amplifies negative banking shocks. By contrast, intensive-margin integration—captured by the diffusion of factoring and invoice discounting—attenuates banking disruptions. The model reveals that the stabilizing effects of integration dominate when firm production linkages are tight. The predictions are consistent with matched bank–firm data from Italy.

title: Turn Down for What

detail.title: Turn Down for What
detail.abstract: This essay focuses on nonjudicial punishment (NJP), which is the predominant form of military justice in the United States. It argues that the "turn down" right, which allows offenders to decline disciplinary proceedings and elect courts-martial instead, is harmful for both military discipline and the rights of military members.

title: Startup Financing and Incumbent Innovation
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Finance

detail.title: Startup Financing and Incumbent Innovation
detail.abstract: I study how startup financing affects innovation beyond the companies it funds. Exploiting the post-1979 expansion in VC supply following ERISA's prudent man clarification, I find that incumbents in industries with greater pre-shock VC exposure increase patenting more after the shock. The response is concentrated among medium-sized firms, which increase patenting across multiple dimensions of innovation. Among these firms, the effect is strongest for those with greater technological capacity and organizational flexibility, suggesting that these capabilities help incumbents translate VC-backed competitive pressure into inventive output. Overall, startup financing shapes technological progress by changing both how much and how incumbents innovate.

title: Human Nature and the Crisis of Civilisation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Human Nature and the Crisis of Civilisation

keywords: Human nature Anthropology Autopoiesis Attention Responsibility Agency Belief Interpretation Civilisation Pragmatism Relationality Structural conditions Flourishing Alienation Low-trust anthropology

detail.abstract: Modern civilisation is in crisis, yet our attempts to solve its problems consistently miss the root cause. This book argues that our deepest crisis is anthropological: we have inherited a low-trust model of human nature and built institutions that systematically reproduce it. Drawing on autopoietic theory and pragmatist philosophy, it develops a functional framework for understanding how beliefs about human nature shape the worlds we inhabit. The question is not "What is human nature?" but "What happens when we believe human nature is this rather than that?" The book traces the hidden anthropology of modern Western civilisation and offers an alternative grounded in participation, responsibility, and care. It concludes that the future depends not on discovering new truths, but on choosing to interpret ourselves differently—and that a different civilisation, once imaginable, becomes possible.

title: Shadow Economy, Tax Revenue and Income Inequality in Africa: A Mediation Analysis
affiliations: , University of Lagos - Department of Economics and State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo

detail.title: Shadow Economy, Tax Revenue and Income Inequality in Africa: A Mediation Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper

detail.abstract: Even though existing studies have extensively investigated the impacts of shadow economic activities and tax revenue on income inequality, the literature overlooks the mediating role of tax revenue in the nexus between the shadow economy and income inequality. In addition, the studies' focus groups have been conducted in high-and middleincome countries. To fill gaps in the existing literature on the nexus between the shadow economy, tax revenue, and income inequality, this study investigates the relationship among the shadow economy, tax revenue, and income inequality. Using an unbalanced panel data set on 48 African countries from 2000 to 2015 and deploying the structural equation modeling (SEM) approach, the empirical results are summarized as follows: (i) for the full sample, shadow economic activities indirectly increase income inequality through decreasing tax revenue. In other words, tax revenue plays a partial mediation role between shadow economic activities and income inequality; and (ii) for the different subregions, tax revenue shows varying mediation effects. For example, the mediation effects of tax revenue in Eastern and Western Africa are similar to those in the full sample of countries. Therefore, based on these findings, we conclude that shadow economic activities are an essential determinant of income inequality. Policy recommendations are put forward.

title: Aligning Through Disagreement: Decision-Influencing Performance Measurement Systems and Cognitive Conflict
affiliations: and University of Galway

detail.title: Aligning Through Disagreement: Decision-Influencing Performance Measurement Systems and Cognitive Conflict
detail.abstract: Performance Measurement Systems (PMSs) are widely used for decision-influencing purposes, motivating employees to align their behaviour with organisational goals. However, despite decision-influencing being one of the central purposes of PMSs, little is known about the behavioural processes through which a decision-influencing use of PMSs achieves this alignment. In this study, we examine how a decision-influencing use of PMSs contributes to cognitive conflict, defined as task-oriented disagreements regarding how performance goals should be achieved. Using survey data from 144 function managers across a range of business functions, we find that the interaction between decision-influencing PMS use and PMS debate is positively associated with cognitive conflict between function managers and senior managers. We also find that cognitive conflict is positively associated with perceived function performance. Overall, our findings identify cognitive conflict as an important behavioural mechanism through which a decision-influencing use of PMSs relates to organisational outcomes.

title: Tokenization Readiness: A Framework for Predicting Which Asset Classes Go On-Chain First

detail.title: Tokenization Readiness: A Framework for Predicting Which Asset Classes Go On-Chain First
detail.abstract: Tokenized RWAs market size grew to $24 billion in a year. We observe that different asset classes tokenize at different speeds. We evaluate this on the basis of two axes; regulatory clarity and legal complexity. We then apply five contrasting asset classes to this framework. We observe that four of these classes confirm that the axes move together like Treasuries and Real Estate. Private Credit and Commodities tokenize quickly under clear and simple conditions. But one asset class remains an exception; Equities has regulatory clarity but remains complex due to operational barriers. On fixing them, tokenization of equities should accelerate rapidly, irrespective of further regulatory change since complexity is the main bottleneck. This framework offers a testable lens for predicting tokenization speed, based on qualitative analysis of publicly available data.

title: Digital Grief and Posthumous Identity: Global Regulatory Gaps in the Era of Griefbots, Posthumous Avatars, and Grief-Oriented Generative AI

detail.title: Digital Grief and Posthumous Identity: Global Regulatory Gaps in the Era of Griefbots, Posthumous Avatars, and Grief-Oriented Generative AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced this study. This work was prepared with the analytical support of Claude (Anthropic); see the Acknowledgements and Declaration on the Use of Generative AI sections of the paper for details
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a comparative legal and regulatory analysis and does not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of primary personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The digital grief industry, comprising griefbots, posthumous voice and image avatars, and virtual reality environments for mourning, has entered the global market at a pace that outstrips the responsiveness of existing regulatory frameworks. This white paper examines the regulatory treatment of grief-oriented generative artificial intelligence across five jurisdictions (the European Union, the United States, China, South Korea and Australia), current as of March 2026. It finds that no national or international framework in force governs these systems in a comprehensive and specific manner. The EU AI Act makes no reference to posthumous identity and would classify griefbots as limited-risk systems subject only to transparency obligations, while the General Data Protection Regulation expressly excludes deceased persons from its scope and delegates the question to Member States, producing a fragmented European landscape. The United States lacks federal regulation. China provides the most developed consent requirements for posthumous likeness, although motivated by content control rather than by protection of the bereaved. Spain offers the principal statutory precedent for a digital will, but one directed at access to accounts rather than at the generative reconstruction of identity. The paper identifies four structural gaps, relating to posthumous consent, the absence of AI-specific digital wills, posthumous dignity, and the allocation of liability, and sets out recommendations for national legislators, international bodies, and industry.

title: From Represented Supply to Effective Market Thickness in Heterogeneous Service Markets

detail.title: From Represented Supply to Effective Market Thickness in Heterogeneous Service Markets
detail.abstract: A market may contain many providers and still offer little usable supply for a particular request. The gap arises because market presence, contemporaneous participation, hard compatibility, and acceptance under offered terms are different economic states. This paper develops effective market thickness as a requestlevel measure of the third state: the number of providers who are represented in the relevant information environment, open to receiving the request at the evaluation episode, and capable of satisfying every hard condition attached to it. The measure is the degree of the request node in a provider-request graph whose effective edges are generated by representation, activity, and feasibility. Its value lies less in the graph operation than in the economic construction of the edge and the staged account of how nominal supply becomes usable supply. The paper derives the basic formal properties of the measure, separates it from willingness, accessibility, capacity, quality, and global allocation, and develops a basis for later measurement, empirical, and diagnostic analysis.

title: The Friction Matrix: A Structural Decomposition of Latin American Productivity

detail.title: The Friction Matrix: A Structural Decomposition of Latin American Productivity
detail.abstract: Latin America has accumulated human and physical capital at rates that should support steady convergence toward the global technological frontier, yet relative labor productivity has stagnated or declined since the 1980s. Standard growth-accounting models consign this shortfall to an abstract Total Factor Productivity residual that names the gap but cannot explain it. Drawing on two decades of operational experience across the region, this paper translates the frictions that businesses face daily—extortion, informal competition, regulatory burden, and benefit-induced labor withdrawal—into a single structural formula: the Friction Matrix. The model expresses relative productivity as the ratio of three productive enablers (human capital, trade integration, governance) to four compounding institutional frictions (informality, insecurity, government weight, and benefit distortion). Calibrated on eight Latin American economies and validated against five out-of-sample countries, the model achieves an 11.48 percent mean absolute error over 2007–2023 with zero country-specific parameters, no dummies, and no adjustments. The results suggest that measurable institutional frictions act as compounding transaction taxes on the formal economy, accounting for approximately 79 percent of the cross-country productivity variance that standard factor-accumulation models leave unexplained, and convert the region's productivity gap into an actionable, friction-by-friction diagnostic.

title:
Outsourcing 2026: Agentic AI and Tier 1 Financial Institutions 
The Delivery-Side Record from 150 Engagements
affiliations: Akholi

detail.title:
Outsourcing 2026: Agentic AI and Tier 1 Financial Institutions 
The Delivery-Side Record from 150 Engagements
detail.abstract:
Between April and June 2026, 850 delivery staff at major outsourcing firms gave this study structured ratings and written testimony. Respondents work on 150 agentic AI outsourcing engagements, serving Tier 1 financial institutions. Their engagements span 10 types of financial institutions and 4 primary outsourcing models. Respondents build the agents. They operate the processes and assemble the client reporting. Their account is vendor-side testimony and uncorroborated by client records.

The study surfaced 4 primary findings:

1.     The industry is new. Every participant is inventing the practice in live engagements. No respondents reported more than 1 year of experience with agentic AI.

2.     Failure is material now. Cancellation is 37.33% for a study set with a median engagement length of 5 months. Client preparation was rated the weakest among all measured factors. Vendor capability rated second weakest. Co-management of the engagement becomes the primary success factor once in production.

3.     The people who assemble client-facing reporting rated it as more likely to be manipulated than accurate. Respondents put the likelihood of manipulation at 6.26 of 10.

4.     Oversight of the agents rests on a junior and dissatisfied workforce that is likely to leave. Respondents rated their job satisfaction at 4.19 out of 10. Most indicated they intend to leave their current job. What holds these engagements together is undocumented knowledge, and departures remove it.

title: Diagnosing False Alpha from Small-Sample Bias In Hurst Exponent Estimation: A Case Study in Estimator Validation, Reproducible Debugging, and Instrument-Specific Signal Behavior

detail.title: Diagnosing False Alpha from Small-Sample Bias In Hurst Exponent Estimation: A Case Study in Estimator Validation, Reproducible Debugging, and Instrument-Specific Signal Behavior
detail.abstract: From February to July 2026, I built a quantitative equity signal system called Entropic, which uses Shannon entropy and the Hurst exponent to identify potentially tradeable patterns in stock price data. An initial backtest produced a BUY signal win rate of 62.2% across 90 resolved signals, a result that passed three independent significance tests. When I ran robustness checks, the win rate collapsed to 35.6%. Investigating why revealed a serious bug: the Hurst estimator was returning values of 0.85-0.95 on pure random walks, when the correct value should be 0.50. This caused the BUY signal to fire on 63% of all observations regardless of actual market conditions. This paper documents that bug, validates a corrected estimator against fractional Brownian motion series across seven known Hurst parameters, and compares four estimation methods: naive R/S (average absolute bias 0.409), Anis-Lloyd corrected R/S (0.346), variance-of-differences on log prices (0.169), and DFA (0.130). After fixing the estimator, a three-year backtest across 4,420 signals produced an overall win rate of 49.7%-no real edge. An exploratory analysis found that BUY signals worked significantly better in momentum-driven stocks like SPY, V, and TSLA (68.1% win rate, p < 0.001, n = 160) than in defensive stocks like GOOGL and UNH (31.8%). That finding is treated as a starting point for future testing, not a confirmed result.

title: Intelligent Energy Demand Forecasting Using Signal Decomposition and Temporal Deep Neural Networks

detail.title: Intelligent Energy Demand Forecasting Using Signal Decomposition and Temporal Deep Neural Networks
detail.abstract: Accurate forecasting of energy demand is a cornerstone of modern grid management, enabling utilities to balance supply and demand, integrate renewable sources, and reduce operational costs. The inherent complexity of electricity consumption patterns—characterized by non-linearity, multi-seasonality, and abrupt changes due to weather or human behavior—poses a significant challenge. Traditional time series models often fail to capture these intricate dynamics, while conventional deep learning approaches can be confounded by noise and non-stationarity. This research introduces a novel hybrid framework that synergistically combines advanced signal decomposition with a specialized temporal deep neural network architecture to achieve superior short-term and mid-term load forecasting accuracy. The methodology begins with a multi-level signal decomposition technique applied to historical load data. By isolating distinct oscillatory modes and the underlying trend, the process effectively filters out high-frequency noise and extracts latent periodicities, transforming a complex, entangled series into a set of more predictable and stationary sub-components. Each of these components is then processed by a dedicated branch of a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) characterized by dilated causal convolutions. This design choice is deliberate: the TCN’s receptive field grows exponentially with network depth, allowing it to capture long-range dependencies and seasonal patterns without the vanishing gradient issues of recurrent networks. Furthermore, an attention mechanism is integrated within each branch to dynamically weight the importance of different temporal features, enabling the model to focus on recent anomalies or specific historical analogs. The processed representations from all branches are fused through a learned weighted aggregation layer, which adaptively determines the contribution of each decomposed signal to the final forecast. The model is trained end-to-end using a composite loss function that combines mean absolute error with a penalty for peak-demand misprediction, ensuring both overall accuracy and operational reliability. Extensive experiments were conducted on high-frequency datasets from three distinct climate zones, including data from residential and industrial sectors. The proposed model was benchmarked against a suite of baselines, including ARIMA, Support Vector Regression, standard Long Short-Term Memory networks, vanilla TCNs, and a plain Transformer. Results demonstrate a consistent and statistically significant reduction in forecast error, with improvements in Mean Absolute Percentage Error ranging from 8.4% to 14.7% over the best-performing deep learning baseline. The decomposition step was shown to be critical, as its removal led to a degradation in performance, particularly during periods of rapid demand fluctuation. The attention maps provided interpretability, revealing that during peak hours, the model heavily weighted high-frequency components from the previous day, while during stable periods, it relied more on the seasonal trend. This hybrid framework effectively addresses the core limitations of applying singular models to complex time series. By separating the forecasting problem into a set of simpler, regularized sub-problems, the model achieves high fidelity without overfitting. The practical implications are substantial: improved demand forecasts allow for more precise unit commitment, reduced spinning reserve requirements, and better integration of stochastic renewable generation. For system operators, the model offers a robust tool that maintains accuracy even under data drift, as the decomposition adapts to new patterns. The architecture is computationally efficient for inference, making it suitable for real-time operational environments. Limitations include the need for careful hyperparameter tuning of the decomposition level and the increased training time compared to simpler models. Future work will explore the integration of exogenous variables such as weather forecasts and economic indicators directly into the decomposed branches, as well as the application of the methodology to probabilistic forecasting for risk management. The findings underscore the profound benefit of preprocessing complex time series data with domain-aware signal processing before feeding it into powerful, yet often opaque, deep learning architectures. This study demonstrates that the thoughtful combination of established analytical techniques with modern neural network designs yields a forecasting system that is both highly accurate and practically adaptable, advancing the state of the art in intelligent energy demand forecasting.

title: Low-Latency Rolling Covariance Estimation in C++: A Streaming Welford Extension with SIMD Dispatch, Condition-Number Analysis, and Empirical Validation

detail.title: Low-Latency Rolling Covariance Estimation in C++: A Streaming Welford Extension with SIMD Dispatch, Condition-Number Analysis, and Empirical Validation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable — this study involved no human participants, patient data, or personally identifiable information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Real-time risk management in trading systems requires maintaining rolling covariance and correlation estimates across many assets, updated on every price tick. The naive approach recomputes covariance over the last K observations from scratch at each tick, an O(K) operation per update. This paper presents an O(1)-per-tick streaming alternative built by extending Welford's algorithm to support a decremental (window-eviction) update alongside the standard incremental update, together with a SIMD-accelerated, runtime-dispatched implementation (scalar / AVX2 / AVX-512) of the resulting M-asset covariance matrix update. We report the full empirical validation process, including two implementation errors discovered through automated testing rather than derivation review: an incorrect algebraic reconstruction in the decremental update, and a hardware-compatibility fault in which forced-path validation code caused an illegal-instruction crash on AVX-512-incapable hardware. We further address, with new empirical evidence, an external correctness critique concerning the numerical stability of the decremental update: we show empirically that error scales with a condition number κ ∼ (µ 2 +σ 2)/σ 2 consistent with the bound of Chan, Golub, and LeVeque (1983), and we verify a log-return preprocessing fix that holds κ near unity independent of price level, reducing absolute error by approximately ten orders of magnitude at equivalent price scale. Finally, we present a memory-traffic optimization (upper-triangular storage exploiting covariance symmetry) that yields a measured 2.00× speedup at M = 512 over a full-matrix layout on real AVX2-only hardware, while being honestly reported as a net slowdown at small M. All results are reproducible; source code, test harnesses, and a real historical-price validation dataset are publicly available.

title: Ensemble VMD-Attention-LSTM Model for Accurate Electricity Load Prediction Under Renewable Energy Integrations

detail.title: Ensemble VMD-Attention-LSTM Model for Accurate Electricity Load Prediction Under Renewable Energy Integrations
detail.abstract: The escalating penetration of variable renewable energy sources into modern power grids introduces unprecedented volatility and non-stationarity in electricity load patterns, rendering conventional forecasting methods increasingly inadequate for ensuring grid reliability, economic dispatch, and operational stability. In response to this critical challenge, this study proposes a novel hybrid deep learning framework—termed Ensemble VMD-Attention-LSTM—that synergistically integrates variational mode decomposition, an attention-enhanced long short-term memory network, and ensemble learning principles to achieve superior accuracy in electricity load prediction under high-renewable scenarios. The methodology systematically addresses three fundamental limitations inherent in existing approaches: the inability to effectively isolate multi-scale oscillatory components from highly non-stationary load signals, the tendency of recurrent architectures to lose long-range dependencies in extended sequences, and the vulnerability of single-model predictions to overfitting in volatile regimes. The proposed framework first applies variational mode decomposition to deconstruct raw electricity load data into a finite set of band-limited intrinsic mode functions, each capturing distinct temporal frequencies ranging from diurnal consumer behavior rhythms to sub-hourly renewable generation transients. This deterministic signal processing step transforms the original chaotic load series into quasi-stationary subcomponents, thereby mitigating the confounding effects of sudden ramping events caused by distributed solar and wind injections. Each decomposed mode is then processed by an independent LSTM network augmented with a multi-head attention mechanism, which dynamically weights the most informative hidden states across the input sequence while suppressing noise and irrelevant historical patterns. The attention mechanism is particularly effective for renewable rich environments where load dependencies shift rapidly due to meteorological forcings, enabling the model to prioritize recent volatility signals over stale baseline patterns. To further enhance robustness against the aleatoric uncertainty inherent in renewable generation, an ensemble strategy is employed where multiple attention-LSTM architectures, each initialized with different random seeds and training data subsamples, are aggregated via a meta learner that optimizes the combinatorial weights through a secondary training phase. This ensemble approach not only reduces prediction variance but also provides inherent uncertainty quantification through the dispersion of individual member forecasts, a critical feature for risk-aware grid operations. The empirical validation of the proposed model is conducted using a comprehensive dataset comprising four years of hourly electricity load measurements from a regional grid characterized by over 40% renewable penetration, including aggregated behind-the-meter solar photovoltaic generation and utility-scale wind farms. The dataset exhibits pronounced non-stationary behaviors, including diurnal and seasonal periodicities, abrupt ramp events triggered by passing weather fronts, and long-term trends from load growth and policy-driven renewable mandates. Extensive comparative benchmarks are performed against a suite of state-of-the-art forecasting models, including standalone LSTM, attention-LSTM without decomposition, VMD-LSTM without attention, standard ensemble methods such as random forests and gradient boosting, and classical time series models including seasonal ARIMA and exponential smoothing. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Ensemble VMD Attention-LSTM model consistently outperforms all baseline methods across multiple evaluation horizons, including one-hour, four-hour, and twenty-four-hour ahead predictions. For the critical day-ahead forecasting task, the proposed framework achieves a mean absolute percentage error of 2.14%, representing relative improvements of 37.8% over standalone LSTM, 24.5% over attention-LSTM without VMD, and 15.2% over VMD-LSTM without attention. Notably, the model exhibits exceptional stability during extreme load events, such as rapid morning ramp ups coinciding with cloud cover changes and evening peaks following wind generation drop-offs, where baseline methods show error inflation of up to 300%. The attention mechanism visualization reveals that the model learns to assign higher weights to recent volatility indicators, such as load values from the past two hours, while appropriately discounting seasonal patterns that become unreliable under high-renewable conditions.

title: Monetary Policy Regimes, Macroeconomic News, and Treasury Excess Returns
affiliations: State University of New York at New Paltz and University of Massachusetts Amherst, Isenberg School of Management, Department of Finance, Students

detail.title: Monetary Policy Regimes, Macroeconomic News, and Treasury Excess Returns

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by CISDM at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst and by SUNY New Paltz.

detail.abstract: We show that the mix of macroeconomic and monetary-policy news that moves daily U.S. Treasury excess returns differs across Chair-defined environments and maturities. General-tospecific models allowing unknown impulses and location shifts identify broad news sensitivity under Greenspan and Bernanke, activity-centered responses under Yellen, and strong inflation and policy-path content under Powell. The sharpest coefficient contrast is the pronounced attenuation of Powell-sample payroll sensitivity, which survives direct cross-sample and leaveone-release-out tests at both maturities. Five-year policy-path symmetry is rejected only under Greenspan, while selected time-varying intercepts are episodic and concentrated around crises and policy transitions.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and CEO of Certavixx Technologies Ltd, a Dubai International Financial Centre company that develops AI assurance software for regulated financial institutions. The company would benefit commercially from regulatory and supervisory approaches of the kind discussed in this paper. No external funding was received for this work, and the views expressed are the author's own.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a policy and regulatory analysis based on publicly available sources; it involves no human participants, personal data, or material requiring ethics approval or consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was undertaken independently by the author.

detail.abstract: The April 2026 revision of US model-risk guidance, SR 26-2, draws a deliberate boundary: generative and agentic AI are outside the guidance, while banks are expected to govern them through broader risk-management arrangements. Two months later, the Financial Stability Board proposed twelve sound practices for responsible AI adoption, including specific controls for autonomous agents. The regulatory problem is therefore no longer an absence of principles. It is the absence of a common regulatory object and an assurance architecture that can convert those principles into evidence of control. This paper proposes that regulators and financial institutions treat a Delegated Decision-and-Action System (DDAS) - not the underlying model alone - as the unit of assurance. It introduces an Agentic Assurance Framework built around authority-based tiering, an explicit agentic control envelope, a pre-deployment assurance case, continuous runtime monitoring, event-triggered revalidation, periodic independent assurance, supervisor-ready evidence and macroprudential monitoring of common dependencies. The framework preserves the strongest ideas of model-risk management - proportionality, independent challenge, validation and accountability - while adapting them to systems that can plan, use tools, maintain state and act in the world. The objective is not more AI paperwork. It is a regulatory design in which institutions can demonstrate, and supervisors can test, that delegated machine authority remains bounded, observable, reversible and accountable.

affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - College of Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

keywords: First And Second Banks of the United States

detail.abstract:
Supporters of the Federal Reserve System (Fed) have long claimed that it should be treated as a ‘fourth branch’ of the federal government that is free from ‘political’ interference by the executive branch. That wish appears to have turned into reality as the result of the Supreme Court’s ruling in Trump v. Cook. There, a majority of the Court (5-4) held that the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 trumped President Donald J. Trump’s (‘47’) removal powers under Article II of the Constitution. The majority ruled that the President could not fire a member of the Fed’s Board of Governors absent a showing of “cause,” as required by that statute. However, the Court simultaneously issued a separate decision in Trump v. Slaughter, in which a majority of the Court (6-3) took the opposite approach for the heads of other “independent” federal agencies such as the Federal Trade Commission. The justification for the special treatment given to Fed board members versus other agency heads was that, for constitutional purposes, the Fed follows in the distinct historical tradition of central bank independence that the majority believed had long coexisted with the President’s Article II powers.

 This article explores that history, which exposed deep fault lines among the Founding Fathers in their earliest attempt to form a government after ratification of the Constitution, and which divided the nation afterwards. The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 was designed to avoid concerns over the independence of a central bank that had led to the demise of the First and Second Banks that are the focus of the Cook decision. The Fed’s supervision proved to be ineffective, and legislation was passed in 1933 and 1935 that increased the Fed’s governmental oversight. However, the Fed remained under the control of the Treasury Department until the Treasury-Fed Accord of 1951. That intra-governmental agreement settled a dispute between the Fed and the Treasury Department over which of them should be responsible for monetary policy. The parties agreed that the Fed would displace the Treasury in that role. The Treasury-Fed Accord was largely honored by fourteen Presidents over the next seventy-five years, albeit not without rancor.

 This article relates this history and questions whether, aside from the removal issue, a gentleman’s agreement in the form of the Treasury-Fed Accord is sufficient to support claims that the Fed has special constitutional powers that a President cannot revoke or changeded the nation.

title: Endogenous Limits to Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Endogenous Limits to Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: Matched prediction contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket trade cents apart for weeks yet rarely settle differently. For binary claims, this arithmetic rules out accounts resting on expected payoff differences. In our model, platforms write distinct contract terms to soften fee competition, and traders sort across venues accordingly. The sorted clienteles exert demand pressure arbitrage cannot undo, since each platform clears its own positions. Contract-term salience is the shared driver of settlement disagreement, volume imbalance, and clientele pressure. The model therefore ranks their correlations. A matched 2026 panel reproduces that ordering coefficient by coefficient. Price integration takes portability, not harmonized wording.

title: Endogenous Limits to Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Endogenous Limits to Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: Matched prediction contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket trade cents apart for weeks yet almost never settle differently, and for binary claims that arithmetic rules out accounts resting on expected payoff differences. In the model developed here, platforms write distinct contract terms to soften fee competition, traders sort accordingly, and the resulting clienteles exert demand pressure that arbitrage cannot undo while positions clear separately per venue. Contractterm salience alone links settlement disagreement, volume imbalance, and clientele pressure, fixing the relative strength of their correlations; a matched 2026 panel reproduces that ranking coefficient by coefficient. Price integration takes portability, not harmonized wording.

title: Marxian Theory of Value and Surplus Value: The Issue of Internal Validity

detail.title: Marxian Theory of Value and Surplus Value: The Issue of Internal Validity
detail.abstract: The paper is devoted to the problem of internal validity of Marx's economic theory. It covers the analysis of the following subjects: the contradiction between two components of commodity-use-value and value-and of the labor that created them; the generation of surplus value; simple and skilled labor; and the moral wear of means of production of the second kind. The close examination of these concepts demonstrates internal inconsistencies in Marxist labor theory of value and surplus value. Marx confuses the use-value with the physical form of a product; the former cannot present itself simultaneously at the private and at the social poles of the commodity. The contradiction of use-value and value, rather than being antagonistic and destructive, plays an overall constructive role in commodity production. Value and surplus value cannot be produced by living labor alone; the organic composition of capital does not determine the amount of surplus value. The difference between skilled and simple labor and the moral wear of means of production, as well as wear and tear of consumer goods, are not consistently explained in the Marxian labor theory of value.

title: The Impact of Political Dynasty to Good Governance in the 5th Congressional District of LEYTE
affiliations: University of San Carlos

detail.title: The Impact of Political Dynasty to Good Governance in the 5th Congressional District of LEYTE
detail.abstract:
The study is a deviation from the usual impact of political dynasties. The research is focused on the good governance aspect amidst the presence of political dynasties. Even before ancient times, when monarchy was the form of government, the word political dynasty did not exist. However, because people crave “freedom,” the type of government was changed to the promise of democracy, and the presence of familial authority became a negative connotation. People should be mindful that the office that these political dynasties held was not through succession but through election (Mapalo, 2015),. Aside from this, governance is not a simple issue; it is a very intricate matter that is essential for one’s existence, primarily for sustainable development.
      Even with the political dynasties in the country, one cannot deny the fact that some of these political leaders have embodied good governance. As the world is getting smaller through the direct interconnectedness of technological globalization, there is a need for cooperation and collaboration for the people’s coexistence. Competition should be lessened, and destructive criticism should be minimized. There is a need to recognize the existence of good governance so as to encourage more public officials to lead the populace with good governance.

title: Reproducible Regional Multipliers from Public Data: Benchmarking a Public-Data FLQ Model Against RIMS II and IMPLAN
affiliations: Capital University - School of Management

detail.title: Reproducible Regional Multipliers from Public Data: Benchmarking a Public-Data FLQ Model Against RIMS II and IMPLAN

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The author purchased the RIMS II data using personal funds. IMPLAN data were accessed through a university academic subscription; no dedicated institutional funding was provided for this study.

keywords: May 2026. Preliminary Working Paper. Comments Welcome Regional Input-Output Analysis

detail.abstract: Regional economic-impact analysis often relies on proprietary systems such as IMPLAN or purchased Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) RIMS II multiplier orders, placing credible screening analysis beyond the reach of many small agencies, nonprofits, students, and independent researchers. This paper develops a reproducible procedure for estimating regional input-output multipliers from public data, using the BEA benchmark Use table and Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) QCEW employment regionalized with Flegg location quotients (FLQ). Unlike recent FLQ and KFLQ studies that evaluate alternative regionalization formulae against survey-based regional tables, this study asks a practitioner-facing question: whether a transparent public-data model can approximate Type II multipliers from both RIMS II and IMPLAN, and at what level of aggregation it ceases to be reliable. The model is benchmarked across Ohio, Franklin County, and the Columbus metropolitan area. At a fifteen-sector aggregation, it approximates Type II output multipliers within roughly 8 to 11 percent of the commercial systems, close to the roughly 8 percent disagreement observed between RIMS II and IMPLAN themselves. At detailed industry level, however, performance deteriorates sharply: employment-based location quotients fail to capture capital-intensive and agriculture-linked supply chains, producing weak rank correlation and large errors for food-processing industries. A county-level imputation experiment recovers suppressed QCEW employment cells but does not materially improve multiplier accuracy. The evidence therefore identifies an application boundary rather than a universally preferred regionalization formula: public data are defensible for broad sector-level impact screening, while industry-detail studies continue to require the regional trade-flow information embedded in commercial systems.
