title: The Hidden Cost of Free Speech: Anti-SLAPP Laws and Firm Productivity
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Hidden Cost of Free Speech: Anti-SLAPP Laws and Firm Productivity
detail.abstract: Does protecting free speech impose costs on firms? We exploit the staggered adoption of U.S. state anti-SLAPP statutes, which shield firms' public critics from retaliatory litigation. Using a stacked differencein-differences design, we find that firm productivity falls 2-3% after adoption. Evidence supports a stakeholder-pressure channel: anti-SLAPP laws increase negative stakeholder-oriented news coverage, expand CSR activities, raise overhead costs, and weaken the sensitivity of investment and hiring to productive opportunities. The productivity decline is larger where stakeholder exposure is greater, managerial discipline weaker, and specialized human capital more important. Our results underscore the tradeoff between public accountability and firm productivity.

title: Chinese Sputnik Moments?
affiliations: Harvard Business School - Finance Unit, Boston University, Kellogg School of Management - Department of Finance, Stanford University and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Chinese Sputnik Moments?
detail.abstract:
China’s technological progress in recent decades has been viewed with admiration, alarm, and (in some cases) doubt. To better understand the Chinese innovation ecosystem, we compile a dataset of almost 14 million domestic Chinese patent publications. We focus on the subset of critical technologies identified by the U.S. Department of Defense. Several surprising patterns emerge from the data: Chinese patenting is strongly associated with other measures of innovative progress; patents are not concentrated in corporate giants such as Huawei; universities have played a key role in innovation, much greater than state-owned enterprises or government-owned facilities; and fewer than one in ten Chinese critical technology patents involves an inventor with U.S. experience or training. Finally, using four text-based measures of patent quality, we show that the rise of Chinese patenting in critical technologies has not been associated with a decline in quality relative to the U.S. awards.

title: The United States and Its Creditors: Assessing Foreign Demand for U.S. Assets
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), Senior Fellow

detail.title: The United States and Its Creditors: Assessing Foreign Demand for U.S. Assets
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes foreign demand for U.S. assets, with particular emphasis on U.S. Treasury securities. It documents compositional shifts in U.S. bilateral external positions across geographic regions and asset classes, providing estimates of creditor positions closer to a nationality-based concept. While rising U.S. equity prices explain a sizable share of the deterioration in the net external position, foreign purchases of U.S. Treasury securities have been the largest source of U.S. current account financing. The share of these securities held by foreign official investors has declined sharply during the past decade, while the share held by foreign private investors (especially through financial centers) has risen. The decline in foreign official holdings is well explained by lower reserve accumulation, increased Federal Reserve holdings, and dollar appreciation against other reserve currencies. The evidence is consistent with central banks rebalancing their portfolios to avoid large swings in currency shares. Geoeconomic fragmentation is negatively correlated with official demand for U.S. Treasuries, while foreign private demand remains sensitive to safe-haven dynamics. Overall, the paper assesses how these structural shifts affect portfolio preferences for U.S. assets and their potential implications for the U.S. external position amid heightened geopolitical and fiscal uncertainty.

title: Meritocracy and the Networks It Forged: China’s Imperial Examination
affiliations: and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - 21st Century China Center

detail.title: Meritocracy and the Networks It Forged: China’s Imperial Examination
detail.abstract:
Institutions that claim to reward merit often also serve as engines that drive the formation of important social networks. We examine this dual role in China’s Imperial Examination, one of history’s longest-lived meritocratic systems. We draw on exam performance data for 24,269 individuals across 112 national examinations in the Qing dynasty (1644–1905) and trace who among them rose to become top officials. Strong exam performance increased the likelihood of attaining high office, but advancement also depended on individuals’ ties to powerful examiners. Because performance and ties to powerful examiners were strongly complementary, individuals’ success appeared to rest on merit even as social networks played a role. Following the major political transformations of the 1840s, the importance of examiner ties persisted, although the influential examiners themselves changed. These findings help explain why such systems retain legitimacy even when networks matter greatly.

title: A Theory of Firm Wage Dynamics
affiliations: IESE Business School and Boston University

detail.title: A Theory of Firm Wage Dynamics
detail.abstract:
We develop a theory of firm wage dynamics that integrates the canonical wage-posting model à la Burdett and Mortensen (1998) with firm dynamics. Firms offer dynamic wage contracts under an equal-treatment constraint in the presence of search frictions. We provide an analytical characterization of equilibrium wage contracts and firm growth as functions only of the distribution of marginal surplus. Consistent with recent empirical evidence, the model implies that (i) firm wages are strongly linked to firm growth but not to firm size; (ii) firm wages decline over the firm life cycle; and (iii) the pass-through of permanent productivity shocks to wages is higher in the short run than in the long run. Firms at the top of the job ladder face excessive labor market competition, so the optimal policy subsidizes their hiring. At the macro level, the optimal policy elevates business dynamism in the steady state, and even more so along the transition.

title: Sharing the Burden: The Impacts of Pharmacy Sector Reforms on the Labor Market for Pharmacists in Portugal
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics, Instituto de Analisis Economico (IAE-CSIC) and

detail.title: Sharing the Burden: The Impacts of Pharmacy Sector Reforms on the Labor Market for Pharmacists in Portugal
detail.abstract:
In the depths of the 2010 financial crisis the Portuguese government enacted a series of reforms in its prescription drug reimbursement system. Over the next three years value added per pharmacist in retail pharmacies fell by a third, reflecting a rise in generic substitution and reductions in the markups allowed for prescription drugs. This massive shock led to pay cuts for incumbent pharmacists and the introduction of a two-tier pay system for new hires, with little or no reduction in the growth of employment. We use detailed longitudinal records from the Quadros de Pessoal data base, merged with information on collective bargaining settlements and firm financial records, to study the impacts of the reforms. We estimate that between 2009 and 2022 average wages of pharmacists fell by a third; most of this reduction was due to lower wages for newly entering cohorts. The implied responsiveness of wages to productivity is substantially above most estimates in the rent-sharing literature, arguably reflecting the strong attachment of workers to the sector and the steady inflow of newly graduating pharmacists. Stepping back, we then consider how wages of pharmacists have diverged relative to wages of other health care professionals in Portugal, and the decisions of recent college applicants to enter the profession.

title: Demand for Safety in the Crypto Ecosystem
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration, City University London - Bayes Business School, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and IESE Business School

detail.title: Demand for Safety in the Crypto Ecosystem
detail.abstract:
We study the demand for safety and liquidity in the crypto ecosystem. We do so under a framework in which a representative investor allocates liquidity across stablecoin deposits in lending pools and traditional safe assets (e.g., MMF shares). Our model delivers three main predictions: (i) the stablecoin deposit premium co-moves with the Treasury premium when investors value the safety and liquidity services of stablecoins; (ii) increases in Treasury supply reduce the stablecoin deposit premium; and (iii) drops in the perceived safety and liquidity of stablecoin deposits (e.g., due to de-pegs or hacker attacks) reduce their premium. Using granular data from hundreds of DeFi pools spanning multiple protocols, tokens, and blockchains, we find evidence supporting these predictions. Investors treat stablecoin deposits as money-like instruments that are borderless and permissionless, yet as fragile as other forms of privately produced safe assets.

title: Time Travel on Professional Profiles
affiliations: , Stanford University - Department of Economics, Revelio Labs and Revelio Labs

detail.title: Time Travel on Professional Profiles
detail.abstract:
Economists increasingly use professional profile data to reconstruct employment histories and measure skill supply. We show that these records are not fixed historical snapshots, but mutable accounts that workers revise over time. Using monthly vintages of Revelio Labs data from 2020–2026, we document that 19.7 percent of established U.S. LinkedIn users retroactively edit the title or description of a job they have already left. These “time-travel” edits are closely tied to labor market transitions: around such edits, workers are much more likely to change employers as compared to later-editing users. This mutability can bias historical measures of skills, but it also reveals workers’ beliefs about which skills are in demand. Retroactive edits show sharp post-2022 increases in AI-related language and recent reductions in work-from-home and DEI language. Finally, LLM-associated writing markers surge after ChatGPT, especially among less-educated groups and MBAs from lower-ranked programs, revealing heterogeneous AI-assisted profile editing.

title: Long-Run Effects of H-1B Immigration on the U.S. Economy
affiliations: Stanford University, Yale University, MIT and Stanford University - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Long-Run Effects of H-1B Immigration on the U.S. Economy
detail.abstract:
We study the effects of H-1B immigration on U.S. industries that employ H-1B workers and their trading partners. Using a novel cross-industry design and the 1999–2003 expansion of the H-1B visa cap for identification, we find that H-1B exposure raised incomes for natives and pre-existing immigrants, with gains concentrated in non-STEM occupations. Income gains propagate forward through supply chains to downstream industries but not backward to upstream industries, consistent with a productivity shock rather than a labor supply shock. We find no direct effect on patenting, suggesting that productivity gains arise from better task execution rather than patentable invention.

title: Improving Financial Literacy: From Corporate Finance to Personal Finance
affiliations: Stanford University - Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research

detail.title: Improving Financial Literacy: From Corporate Finance to Personal Finance
detail.abstract:
This article provides an overview of the literature on financial literacy. It covers the initial measurement that created the Big Three questions and measures of personal finance knowledge featuring 28 questions. It shows that levels of financial literacy are low and have not been improving over time. This is true not only in the United States but also in countries worldwide. These findings matter because financial literacy is conducive to savvy financial behaviors, from holding precautionary savings to planning for retirement to many other financial decisions. Financial education programs have grown exponentially over time, providing important insights into their cost-effectiveness. Personal finance courses have been added to high school and college curricula, and the evidence indicates that they are useful initiatives to improve financial knowledge and downstream behavior.

title: Unpacking Treatment Effect Heterogeneity in a Large-Scale Dropout-Prevention Experiment
affiliations: Stanford University, Department of Economics, University of Notre Dame, Cornell University, University of Notre Dame and University of Notre Dame - Department of Economics and Econometrics

detail.title: Unpacking Treatment Effect Heterogeneity in a Large-Scale Dropout-Prevention Experiment
detail.abstract:
Timely high school completion is a critical step in successful transitions to post-secondary schooling and the labor market. This randomized controlled trial, deployed in two urban, disadvantaged school districts, tests the effectiveness of a mature and comprehensive student-support program on an unusually large scale (n=2,528). While overall effects on graduation rates are small and statistically insignificant, exploratory analyses reveal notable variation by site and over time, mirroring heterogeneity in treatment timing and program implementation. These findings highlight the challenges of scaling interventions and raise concerns about generalizing results from small-scale, single-site evaluations.

title: The Anatomy of Tariff Pass-through into Consumer Prices
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University - Graduate School of Arts and Sciences - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Anatomy of Tariff Pass-through into Consumer Prices
detail.abstract:
Tariffs raise the prices of goods made at home, not just the imports they tax—an effect that standard pass-through estimates largely miss. Studying the 2025 U.S. tariffs, we find that about 26 percent of the tariff increase passes through to consumer prices. These estimates are measured relative to less-exposed goods and hold aggregate conditions fixed. The direct effect accounts for 64 percent of this increase, as tariffs raise the consumer prices of foreign varieties of a good. The remaining 36 percent arises indirectly—tariffs raise the cost of imported inputs used by U.S. producers, and domestic producers raise their markups because they face less competition from higher-priced imports. The direct effect passes through quickly, since tariffs raise import prices almost immediately, but the indirect effect takes nine to twelve months to work its way through supply chains. As a result, tariffs have a larger and more drawn-out impact on consumers than the direct effect alone would suggest.

title: Replaceable but Employed: Automation and the Meaning of Work
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Replaceable but Employed: Automation and the Meaning of Work
detail.abstract:
Can automation harm workers without replacing them? We study jobs in which workers value both producing useful output and knowing that the output depends on their own contribution. A credible machine alternative can weaken that second source of meaning even when the firm retains the worker. Our model shows that this loss raises compensation when wages adjust fully; when they adjust only partly, workers bear some of the loss themselves. It can also make automation more likely. An external developer may profit by publicly demonstrating a machine before licensing it, because the demonstration lowers the value of the human alternative. This "meaning externality" can create demand for the machine and make profitable development socially harmful. Better technical quality and greater public salience have different effects: quality improves output, while salience alone weakens human work. Automation can, therefore, reduce the value of work before it eliminates jobs.

title: Monetary Policy in Mandarin Capitalism
affiliations: and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Monetary Policy in Mandarin Capitalism
detail.abstract:
This paper investigates why China’s recurrent credit expansions have coincided with persistently weak inflation. We argue that this pattern reflects the country’s production-oriented monetary regime. At the aggregate level, faster monetary-financial expansion temporarily raises PPI inflation but depresses it over longer horizons. At the sectoral level, liability growth among listed industrial firms is followed by weaker producer prices, lower profitability, higher leverage, rising inventories, and reduced capacity utilization. We also find asymmetric supply-chain transmission: downstream liability growth raises upstream PPI inflation, while upstream liability growth does not generate a corresponding downstream price response. These findings indicate that credit expansion in China tends to sustain production and balance sheets rather than stimulate final demand. As a result, monetary policy operates less as a conventional tool for demand management and durable reflation, and more as a mechanism for preserving production capacity and supporting growth.

title: Common Ownership and Collusion
affiliations: , Boston University - Markets, Public Policy, and Law and University College Dublin

detail.title: Common Ownership and Collusion
detail.abstract:
We provide the first empirical evidence that common ownership can facilitate explicit collusion. Our unique setting, the population of legal cartels in Sweden, lets us observe cartel formation, duration, and dissolution without the sample-selection bias that plagues studies of detected cartels. Combining hand-collected ownership data with the universe of registered cartels, we compute firm-pair profit weights (κ) that measure how much one firm internalizes a rival's profits. Higher profit weights are associated with a greater likelihood of cartel participation, predict future cartel involvement, and are linked to longer cartel duration. Firms also reduce their profit weights immediately after a cartel dissolves. However, this relationship is concentrated among pairs in which the firm that internalizes the rival firm's profits colludes while the rival does not. Common ownership therefore complements a firm’s own participation in explicit collusion but substitutes for cartel participation by the rival whose profits it internalizes.

title: Incomplete Information and Self-Fulfilling Inflation Dynamics—Lucas meets Keynes
affiliations: New York University - Leonard N. Stern School of Business - Department of Economics, Peking University HSBC Business School and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), Antai College of Economics and Management, Students

detail.title: Incomplete Information and Self-Fulfilling Inflation Dynamics—Lucas meets Keynes
detail.abstract:
This paper incorporates the Lucas (1973) island model into a standard DSGE framework. It demonstrates that self-fulfilling stochastic inflation equilibria, which are driven by intrinsic uncertainty or pure sentiments, can exist under rational expectations. Furthermore, it shows that these sentiment-driven stochastic equilibria exhibit monetary non-neutrality, even when the fundamental equilibrium is unique and monetarily neutral. As the aggregate price or inflation rate can appear to fluctuate independently of the money supply, our model explains the complex relationship between inflation and the money supply in the real world, where the basic quantity theory of money often seems invalid.

title:
Do Time Series Foundation Models Know Their Tails? 

A Mechanism-Oriented, Contamination-Aware Audit of Zero-Shot Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall

Do Time Series Foundation Models Know Their Tails? 

A Mechanism-Oriented, Contamination-Aware Audit of Zero-Shot Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall

detail.abstract: Can zero-shot time series foundation models supply reliable tail-risk forecasts? Under a contamination-aware, pre-specified protocol we audit Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall from five deployed heads on 32 daily series across extraction rules, regimes, and training-free repairs. Native deep tails are structurally unusable or extraction-dependent. The diagnosis is organized by two within-family contrasts (Chronos-2's quantile head versus Chronos-Bolt's bounded grid versus Chronos-base's token-sampling head, and Moirai-1.1's mixture head versus Moirai-2.0's quantile head) and one cross-form contrast (Moirai-2.0's quantile head versus Lag-Llama's parametric Student-t head). The contrasts are associative, not causal; the token-sampling head suffers an order-of-magnitude scale collapse no extraction rule repairs, and regime failures are head-specific. Replacing the conditional scale is decisive; location is second-order at the daily one-step horizon. A TSFM-location/GARCH-scale hybrid meets the pre-specified criterion on all five core heads and matches, does not exceed, classical GARCH-EVT. Forecast form, not model label, comes first in a tail-risk audit.

title: Childhood Cognitive and Behavioral Impairments and Adult Health
affiliations: , Princeton University and Rutgers University, New Brunswick - Robert Wood Johnson Medical School

detail.title: Childhood Cognitive and Behavioral Impairments and Adult Health
detail.abstract:
We use U.S. nationally representative longitudinal data to estimate the effects of cognitive and behavioral impairments in childhood on health in adulthood. We focus on work-limiting health conditions and fair or poor self-rated health but also consider adequacy of sleep, body weight, and health behaviors (use of various substances and preventive health care) as potential pathways. In household fixed effects models, we find that both impairments are strongly associated with having a work-limiting health condition in adulthood; specifically, cognitive impairments increase the probability of a work-limiting condition by 70% and behavioral impairments increase the probability by 60%. Individuals with cognitive impairments in childhood are 43% more likely to report being in fair or poor health in adulthood compared to individuals without cognitive impairments. The effects of cognitive impairments on health do not appear to operate through insufficient sleep, obesity, or health behaviors. Individuals with childhood behavioral impairments are no more likely to report being in fair or poor health but are more likely to get insufficient sleep and to be obese, compared to individuals without behavioral impairments, suggesting that insufficient sleep and obesity could potentially lie on the pathway from behavioral impairments in childhood to work-limiting health conditions in adulthood.

title: The Value of Behavioral Policies
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Bocconi University, Australian National University (ANU) and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: The Value of Behavioral Policies
detail.abstract:
Behavioral interventions have become central to modern public policy, but their empirical promise remains contested because estimated treatment effects often appear small. We argue that a policy response is economically meaningful only relative to the response generated by alternative policies. We assemble more than 1,200 estimates from over 600 studies comparing “nudges” and traditional price interventions in the markets for cigarettes, alcohol, influenza vaccination, electricity, and residential water. Translating nudge effects into equivalent price changes, we find that behavioral interventions often correspond to enormous fiscal interventions, from an 11% tax on electricity to a 100% subsidy on influenza vaccinations. Nudges are also more cost-effective than price instruments in all markets, but cost-effectiveness does not predict the welfare ranking of policies. Using a behavioral extension of the Marginal Value of Public Funds, we show that nudges have high welfare returns at the margin, while price instruments often generate larger total surplus at scale.

title: The Economics of Civil Service Protections
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business

detail.title: The Economics of Civil Service Protections
detail.abstract:
The study of bureaucracy as a key dimension of state capacity has gained increasing attention in economics. What organizational features create an effective bureaucracy, however, remains subject to debate. This paper focuses on the central role of civil service protections in delineating the boundary between politics and administration. I introduce a simple principal-agent framework to discuss the key theoretical channels through which political insulation can shape bureaucrat performance. Guided by the framework, I establish stylized facts and organize evidence from historical and contemporary civil service reforms. Overall, the micro-level evidence documents a positive effect of civil service protections on the quality of public service delivery. I conclude with open questions about the political economy of reform adoption.

title: From Barrels to Balance Sheets: The Role of Accounting in Saudi Aramco's Sustainability Strategy to Net-Zero
affiliations: Arkansas State University

detail.title: From Barrels to Balance Sheets: The Role of Accounting in Saudi Aramco's Sustainability Strategy to Net-Zero
detail.abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive analysis of Saudi Aramco's sustainability accounting practices and offers insights into how the world's largest integrated oil and gas company manages the challenges of environmental responsibility and energy transition. Through a multi-faceted examination of Aramco's strategies, the study explores the intersection of sustainability, technology, and corporate governance in the oil and gas sector. The research employs a mixed-method approach by combining qualitative analysis of corporate reports with quantitative text analysis using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques. It examines Aramco's carbon accounting framework, ESG integration, and technological innovations in sustainability reporting. The study also presents a comparative analysis with other major players like ADNOC and ExxonMobil to highlight industry trends and best practices. Theoretical perspectives, including legitimacy, stakeholder, and institutional theories, are applied to interpret Aramco's actions that reveal complex and sometimes contradictory forces shaping its sustainability strategy. Key findings indicate Aramco's significant strides in integrating advanced technologies such as AI, blockchain, and IIoT into its sustainability accounting, improving data accuracy and reporting reliability. The company's multi-tiered ESG governance structure demonstrates a commitment to embedding sustainability at all decision-making levels. However, the lack of comprehensive Scope 3 emissions reporting remains a notable gap. The chapter concludes by discussing implications for industry and policymakers.

title: Sanctions and Structural Change: Evidence from Iran's Resistance Economy under Maximum Pressure
affiliations: Brigham Young University

detail.title: Sanctions and Structural Change: Evidence from Iran's Resistance Economy under Maximum Pressure
detail.abstract: Economic sanctions are widely used as a foreign policy tool to weaken adversarial states, but their effects on the structure of a targeted economy—rather than its aggregate output—remain understudied. This paper examines whether the 2018 U.S. "Maximum Pressure" sanctions on Iran altered the composition of Iran's economy, specifically its manufacturing share of GDP. Using the synthetic control method, I construct a counterfactual "Synthetic Iran" from a donor pool of middle-income and resource-dependent economies (with the largest weights assigned to Türkiye, Kazakhstan, and Oman) that closely reproduces Iran's pre-treatment manufacturing trajectory from 2000–2017. Following the reimposition of sanctions in 2018, Iran's manufacturing share diverges sharply from its synthetic counterpart, rising by roughly 4–7 percentage points in the post-treatment period. This divergence is robust to alternative pre-treatment windows, simplified predictor sets, and the exclusion of high-weight donor countries, and it survives both placebo-in-space and falsification tests. The results suggest that sanctions did not merely suppress Iranian economic activity but reshaped its composition, consistent with the Iranian regime's promotion of a "resistance economy" emphasizing import substitution and reduced reliance on global markets. These findings contribute to the sanctions literature by highlighting a structural adaptation margin largely absent from existing work, and carry a policy implication: as targeted economies reorganize around domestic production, their exposure to the global financial and trade networks through which sanctions operate may narrow, potentially limiting the long-run coercive effectiveness of broad-based economic pressure.

title: The Protective Power of Connectivity: Internet Exposure and Intimate Partner Violence
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad,  and Jindal School of Government and Public Policy, O. P. Jindal Global University

detail.abstract: We study the effect of women’s exposure to the internet on the incidence of intimate partner violence using data from a large-scale nationally representative data for India. Utilizing an instrumental variable approach, we exploit the exogenous variation arising from cellular tower density at the district level as an instrument. We find that women who have access to the internet are at a significantly lower risk of exposure to physical, sexual, emotional and any IPV by 15, 5, 8 and 17 percentage points. We provide further indicative evidence that attitudes justifying violence and employment work as channels of our estimated impacts. Our results are robust to sensitivity checks, additional controls, alternative definitions and falsification analysis. We document heterogeneity across social groups, wealth index, area of residence, and women’s education levels with the effect being particularly important for the more educated women and for those from the marginalized social groups.

title: Nickel and DIMEd - Trading DIME's "Participation Awards" for Mutually Reinforcing Capabilities
affiliations: King's College London

detail.title: Nickel and DIMEd - Trading DIME's "Participation Awards" for Mutually Reinforcing Capabilities

detail.abstract:
For decades, the dominant cognitive model for U.S. national security statecraft has been DIME (Diplomacy, Information, Military, Economics), which has iteratively bloated into acronyms like DIMEFIL and MIDFIELD. This paper demonstrates that DIME does not clarify national power; rather, it fractures statecraft by categorizing capabilities by bureaucratic agency zip code—functioning as an interagency "participation award" that breeds administrative silos. 


Tracing the philosophical divide between Jominian "addition" and Clausewitzian "admixture" (rooted in contested translations of On War regarding Clausewitz's use of Beimischung), the paper shows how structural isolation undermines grand strategic execution. To replace this fragmented paradigm, the paper revives and expands upon a forgotten 1918 U.S. Army General Staff study: the PPCE framework (Political, Psychological, Combat, Economic).


Operating across three interlocking layers, the PPCE construct maps national power to functional, mutually reinforcing effects suspended within an environmental matrix of Information and Time. Synthesizing strategic theory from Sun Tzu, Liddell Hart, John Boyd, and Colin Gray, this working paper provides a diagnostic blueprint for interagency planning and professional military education. Ultimately, it argues that overcoming bureaucratic inertia requires active executive enforcement to transform statecraft from compartmentalized addition into a synthesized admixture of national power

title: Quantifying the Tail Risk Miscalibration of Geometric Brownian Motion: A Cross-Sectional Empirical Study via the Tail Coverage Ratio
affiliations: , Synthica Research Group, Synthica Research Group and Synthica Research Group

detail.title: Quantifying the Tail Risk Miscalibration of Geometric Brownian Motion: A Cross-Sectional Empirical Study via the Tail Coverage Ratio
detail.abstract: We test how far the normality assumption in Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM) distorts equity tail-risk estimates. GBM is calibrated to five large-capitalization stocks (AAPL, AMZN, GOOGL, MSFT, TSLA) on a four-year daily window (April 2021 to April 2025), with the final year held out. We introduce the Tail Coverage Ratio (TCR), the ratio of realized to GBM-predicted breach frequency, which equals one under correct calibration. Two results follow, pointing in opposite directions. Every TCR estimate falls below one (means of 0.462 at 95% and 0.558 at 99%): thresholds calibrated on a turbulent window and applied to a calmer holdout were crossed less often than predicted. Yet every Expected Shortfall ratio also falls below one (means of 0.876 and 0.728): when a breach did occur, the realized loss exceeded the GBM expectation. The frequency result is driven mainly by regime mismatch and the severity result by the Gaussian tail; we keep the two channels separate and identify the tests that would isolate each.

title: Decaying Capacity: Taxation under Autocratic and Democratic Regimes in Indonesia, 1984-2024
affiliations: Ministry of Finance - Indonesia

detail.title: Decaying Capacity: Taxation under Autocratic and Democratic Regimes in Indonesia, 1984-2024

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I work at The Ministry of Finance Republic of Indonesia

detail.abstract: This article examines the process of decaying tax capacity and relates this decay with change of political regime. Using Indonesia as case study, I consider that persistent declines in tax collection, interspersed with episodes of collapsing revenue, is the symptom of a decaying tax capacity. Drawing upon the comparative literature on taxation and political regime as well as on the review of regulatory evolution, I propose three stages of decaying tax capacity, particularly of a country that transited from autocracy to (incomplete) democracy. In the first stage an autocrat may implement a successful tax reform. In the second stage tax incentives begin to creep in, buoyed by favorable conditions built during the previous stage. In the third stage the incentives become excessive and hard to reverse, decaying the ability of the tax system to perform its revenue function.

title:
Difference-in-Differences with Spillovers: 
An Imputation Approach
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics and Renmin University of China, School of Business

detail.title:
Difference-in-Differences with Spillovers: 
An Imputation Approach
detail.abstract: Staggered difference-indifferences designs typically rule out interference: a unit's outcome may not depend on other units' adoption. In many policy settings this fails, and the policy question is itself about interference-what is the effect of adopting a policy when one's neighbors or competitors have already adopted it, relative to adopting alone? This within-unit interaction between own adoption and exposure to others' adoption is the headline estimand of this paper. Recent nonparametric work identifies own-adoption effects holding exposure fixed (Xu, 2026) and untreated-state spillover effects learned from never-treated units (Tagawa, 2026), and shows that treated-state spillover objects-and hence the interaction-are not point-identified under exposure-conditional parallel trends alone. We supply economically motivated structure under which the interaction is point-identified: spillover pressure proportional to neighbors' dynamic direct effects, with additive level and interaction incidence parameters (γ 1 , γ 2). Estimation extends the imputation approach of Borusyak et al. (2024): unit and period effects are fitted on doubly-clean observations (neither treated nor exposed), imputed composite effects are then fitted by a bilinear least-squares stage computed by alternating least squares. We give constructive identification conditions in terms of a four-cell support condition on the rollout, characterize the bias of spillover-blind estimators, propose full-pipeline wild cluster bootstrap inference, and develop specification tests-including a second-ring placebo and a nonparametric exposure-cell cross-check-that discipline the added structure.

title: North Korea and the United Nations

detail.title: North Korea and the United Nations
detail.abstract: North Korea's membership in the United Nations (UN) has been a source of constant tension and frustration. Despite being a member state for over three decades, North Korea has consistently defied international norms and pursued a nuclear weapons program, undermining the UN's mission of promoting peace and security.

title: Regional Integration and the Balance of Trade in ECOWAS: Evidence from Nigeria and Benin Republic
affiliations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University

detail.title: Regional Integration and the Balance of Trade in ECOWAS: Evidence from Nigeria and Benin Republic
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how regional integration within the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) affects the balance of trade between Nigeria and Benin Republic, two economies bound by an asymmetric but historically deep trading relationship. Using annual panel data spanning 1990-2023 on trade openness, tariff rates, real GDP, and population growth, the study applies a fixed-effects panel OLS estimator, following unit root and Pedroni cointegration testing. Trade openness is found to have a positive and statistically significant relationship with the balance of trade (elasticity of 0.88), while tariff rate exhibits a negative and marginally significant relationship. Population growth shows an unexpected negative association, and real GDP is positively and significantly related to trade balance. The results imply that deepening regional trade integration improves Nigeria and Benin's aggregate trade position, but tariff liberalisation without complementary industrial policy can widen import dependence for the less industrialised partner. The paper recommends targeted investment in agriculture, manufacturing, and export diversification, alongside full implementation of the ECOWAS Common External Tariff and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), to help both economies capture the gains from integration more equitably.

title: The Spirit of Law and the Source of Its Legitimacy

detail.title: The Spirit of Law and the Source of Its Legitimacy
detail.abstract:
This work comprises two complementary parts that systematically examine the foundations of legal order. Part I, "The Source of Legitimacy for Legal Institutions," asks: whence derives the authority of procedural justice? Drawing on legal positivism, social contract theory, and the Radbruch Formula, and supported by SIPRI global military expenditure data, United Nations currency system statistics, and Tom Tyler's empirical procedural justice research, it argues that procedural authority is delegated rather than inherent, and that its legitimacy depends on sustained service to substantive justice. 

Part II, "What Is the Spirit of Law?" asks: when procedure and substance diverge, what should the spirit of law be? Drawing on system justification theory, the trolley problem moral experiments, Kant's categorical imperative, and Mozi's doctrine of impartial care, and supported by Edelman Trust Barometer data, it argues that the spirit of law consists in the isomorphic evolution of individual and whole-the structural reciprocity of "all for one, one for all." The two parts form a progressively deepening argument: the source of legitimacy explains why authority merits obedience, while the spirit of law answers where authority should be directed.

title: Housing Bust and Long-Term Human Capital Scarring in the U.S.
affiliations: TBS Business School and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Housing Bust and Long-Term Human Capital Scarring in the U.S.
detail.abstract: We document persistent human capital scarring among the children of homeowners who reached college age during the 2008-2011 housing bust. Negative shocks to parental housing wealth substantially reduced college attendance among first-year college-age children of homeowners, relative to their counterparts from renter households. In regions experiencing the largest declines in housing wealth, the educational gap between the offspring of homeowners and renters persisted for at least a decade. The shortfall in human capital accumulation translated into lower long-run employability, particularly in education-intensive sectors, and resulted in lower earnings among the affected cohort.

title:
An Endogenous Regime-Switching Model of Capitalist Economic Dynamics 
(A Disequilibrium Static Model)

detail.title:
An Endogenous Regime-Switching Model of Capitalist Economic Dynamics 
(A Disequilibrium Static Model)
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a theoretical model of the fundamental dynamics of a capitalist economy by 
explaining expansion, recession, and recovery as transitions between distinct regimes of firm behavior. 
The basic structure of the model is grounded in the theory of crises developed by Kōzō Uno. 
In this model, capital accumulation continues during an expansion despite a decline in profitability, but 
is ultimately brought to a halt by a sharp increase in the interest rate. The distortions accumulated during 
the expansion subsequently trigger a transition to recession. During the recessionary regime, expected 
demand becomes the principal constraint on production and investment, and technological innovation 
becomes the essential condition for economic recovery. 
Rather than treating equilibrium as a state that is instantaneously realized, this model regards 
equilibrium as a structural relation that persists throughout the dynamic movement of the economy. This 
perspective makes it possible to explain both business cycles and firm behavior during recessions. The model reformulates, rather than simply rejects, the equilibrium theory of classical economics.
Although this paper presents the framework as a "Disequilibrium Static Model," it differs fundamentally 
from conventional comparative statics. Each regime is formulated as a locally stable structural state rather 
than a fully realized equilibrium, while switches in firms' behavioral principles generate transitions 
between regimes.

title: Compliance by Algorithm: Regulatory Technology, Corporate Accountability, and the Institutional Reconstruction of Financial Governance

detail.title: Compliance by Algorithm: Regulatory Technology, Corporate Accountability, and the Institutional Reconstruction of Financial Governance

keywords.keywords: Artificial intelligence governance; algorithmic compliance; regulatory technology (RegTech); corporate compliance; financial regulation; algorithmic accountability; automated decision-making; corporate governance; model risk management; comparative law; EU AI Act; compliance-washing; finan

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has fundamentally transformed corporate compliance from a human-centered governance function into an algorithmically mediated system of regulatory interpretation. This article examines the accountability gap that emerges when AI-driven compliance systems autonomously identify, prioritize, or authorize regulatory decisions within financial institutions. It argues that existing legal frameworks remain fragmented, addressing automated decision-making through separate regimes of data protection, prudential supervision, securities regulation, and horizontal AI legislation, without establishing a unified doctrine of institutional responsibility for algorithmic compliance failures. Employing a comparative legal methodology, the study analyzes regulatory and judicial developments across the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, Singapore, Brazil, and China, integrating doctrinal analysis, jurisprudence, and empirical evidence from recent supervisory enforcement actions and regulatory reports. The findings reveal that contemporary regulatory models govern algorithmic inputs and outputs while largely neglecting the intermediary process of algorithmic legal interpretation, thereby enabling "compliance-washing" and obscuring institutional accountability. To address this structural deficiency, the article proposes the Verifiable Algorithmic Compliance Standard (VACS), an attribution-based governance framework that conditions the regulatory benefits of automated compliance on demonstrable traceability between algorithmic outputs and accountable human oversight. The proposed model seeks to strengthen transparency, reinforce corporate governance, and establish a coherent legal architecture for AI-enabled compliance systems in an increasingly automated financial ecosystem.

reference: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Research Paper No. 17/2026
title: The Effects of Labour Laws on Productivity, Employment, Unemployment and the Labour Share of National Income: Analysis of New Evidence From the Cambridge Leximetric Database, with a UK-China Comparison
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Centre for Business Research (CBR) and University of Cambridge - Judge Business School

detail.title: The Effects of Labour Laws on Productivity, Employment, Unemployment and the Labour Share of National Income: Analysis of New Evidence From the Cambridge Leximetric Database, with a UK-China Comparison

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Research Paper No. 17/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We report the results of an econometric analysis of the effects of labour laws in the UK and China. For data on labour laws we draw on the 2023 update of the CBR-LRI index, part of the Cambridge Leximetric Database, which codes for labour laws around the world between 1970 and 2022. The longitudinal coverage of the CBR-LRI enables us to use time-series techniques which model dynamic changes in an economy over time. We employ impulse response function analysis to estimate the effects of labour laws on indicators of efficiency (productivity, employment and unemployment) and distribution (labour’s share of national income). We find that stronger labour laws in the UK are associated with rising employment and falling unemployment, while those in China are associated with rising productivity. We also observe positive impacts of labour laws on the labour share in both countries. Breaking down our results according to particular types of labour law, the positive employment effect we see in the UK is associated with stronger working time protections, while the positive productivity effect in China is associated with more protective laws regulating flexible forms of employment and with stronger dismissal laws.

A large literature has studied the drivers of these fluctuations, including total factor productivity shocks, world interest rate shocks, and terms-of-trade disturbances.
