detail.abstract: Institutional responses to generative artificial intelligence in education have converged on a documentation paradigm: policies specify when AI use must be disclosed, how it must be cited, and what penalties follow nondisclosure. This paper argues that the paradigm rests on a category error. The problem generative AI poses to education is not a documentation problem but a measurement problem: the student artifact, the essay, the problem set, the take-home assessment, no longer reliably indicates whether the understanding it was designed to evidence actually exists in the student. The paper introduces a three-axis taxonomy of academic integrity (disclosure, verification, and compositional integrity) and shows that current policy addresses only the first while the crisis lives in the third. It then develops a mechanism for the failure, borrowed fluency: generative AI supplies articulacy that is subjectively indistinguishable from comprehension at the moment it is received, collapsing the friction that historically forced learners to convert borrowed material into their own knowledge. Because the traditional markers of integration, above all the stylistic seam between a student's voice and imported material, have lost their signaling value and in some respects inverted, the gap between artifact quality and demonstrated understanding is widening, and it is widening adversarially, in ways that improved artifact-side detection cannot repair. The paper closes by deriving the single property any valid repair must preserve, a cost differential between students who have converted material and students who have not, and by offering three falsifiable predictions, one of which is constructed so that the paper's central mechanism can be proven wrong.

title:
Capitalization As a Means, Not an End: Article 56 Of Ordinance MTP No. 1,467/2022 And Mass Segregation as an Efficient Adjustment of the Financial Regime in Brazilian Public Servants' Pension Schemes (RPPS) 

Evidence From 20 Brazilian Municipalities, 2010 To 2025
affiliations: , Center for Finance and Retail Studies, FIA Business School and University of Sao Paulo, Retail Management Program

detail.title:
Capitalization As a Means, Not an End: Article 56 Of Ordinance MTP No. 1,467/2022 And Mass Segregation as an Efficient Adjustment of the Financial Regime in Brazilian Public Servants' Pension Schemes (RPPS) 

Evidence From 20 Brazilian Municipalities, 2010 To 2025
detail.abstract: Funding (capitalization) is, in Brazilian public servants' pension schemes (RPPS), a means to financial and actuarial balance, not an end. This article argues that its full application to single pension plans, under article 56 of Ordinance MTP No. 1,467/2022, overburdens the fiscal capacity of federative entities by requiring the immediate funding of a deficit that is mostly inherited from the past. With the end of the phase-in set by Ordinance MPS No. 861/2023, the requirement that the amortization contribution exceed the deficit's interest becomes full from 2027 onwards, which heightens the urgency of the matter. Through documentary analysis of 20 mass-segregation implementation studies in municipal RPPS from five federative units, covering the 2010 to 2025 period, the article examines the alternative of matching the financial regime to the nature of each group: funding for the balanced group, in the Funded Account, and pay-as-you-go for the inherited liability, in the Pay-As-You-Go Account. In 18 of the 20 cases, the Funded Account turns out balanced or in surplus, isolating the deficit in the Pay-As-You-Go Account; in all 20, the studies conclude that the measure is fiscally advantageous to the entity. This advantage stems mainly from the temporal redistribution of the cost and from better compliance with the fiscal limits, not from a reduction in the present value of the total cost. The conclusion is that mass segregation is the most efficient and economical means of funding the inherited deficit, while fully preserving the commitment to the insured.

title: A High-Resolution Economic and Hydrological Analysis of the Rewetting of Agricultural Peatlands in Southern Germany for Climate Change Mitigation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Freiburg, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Hohenheim, University of Hohenheim, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A High-Resolution Economic and Hydrological Analysis of the Rewetting of Agricultural Peatlands in Southern Germany for Climate Change Mitigation
detail.abstract: Drained peatlands account for around four per cent of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The EU is the second largest emitter worldwide, with Germany having the highest emissions within the EU. Protecting peatlands in the EU, and in Germany in particular, is therefore a key priority in terms of climate policy. In Germany, agriculture is the dominant land use in terms of drained peatlands, and rewetting them can therefore pose particular challenges and be associated with substantial economic impacts on farms in highly productive regions. We have therefore focused on the GHG reduction potential and farm economic impacts of a large-scale rewetting of agricultural peatlands in Upper Swabia (districts of Biberach, Bodenseekreis, Ravensburg and Sigmaringen), a region in Baden-Württemberg characterized by intensive dairy farming on the border with Bavaria and Austria. A key feature of the analysis was the highly spatially resolved integrated economic and hydrological modelling approach, which we believe to be unique in the southern German context. This enabled us to consider the interplay between local factors such as the spatial configuration and location of peatlands, site-specific hydrological conditions, and plot-specific land use on a regional scale. Methodologically the geodata-based economic model PALUD was coupled with the hydrological model RoGeR. Based on site-specific groundwater levels modeled with RoGeR in a scenario with drainage (reference) and without drainage to raise the groundwater level (peatland rewetting scenario), the achievable GHG reduction through rewetting was calculated and transferred to PALUD. Depending on a model-derived payment for each avoided t CO2eq on the peatland areas, the results showed that with payments between 100 and 200 € per t CO2eq, between approximately 50% and nearly 100% of the maximum GHG reduction potential of approx. 282,333 t CO2eq a-1 on the peatland areas could be realized. While the economic impact at sector level was relatively low, the model results showed considerable effects on individual farms under the assumptions made. For instance, approximately 9% of farms with land on organic soils lost over 30% of their gross margin when around 50% of the considered peatland area was rewetted. The economic effects on individual farms depended highly on the proportion of land on peatlands. Moderate GHG abatement costs can thus lead to substantial income losses for individual farms and pose a significant obstacle to large-scale peatland rewetting. A forward-looking strategic land management could be essential, such as creating land pools to reserve exchange land for affected farms. Further research is also needed on economically viable land-use concepts for rewetted peatlands, as well as on their socioeconomic impacts. Our analyses provide a solid foundation for decision-making in agricultural and environmental policy in Baden-Württemberg, as well as in other regions with intensive dairy farming and peatlands.

title: How Managed Lake-Level Fluctuations Affect Waterfront Property Values: Evidence from a Regulated Lake System
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Managed Lake-Level Fluctuations Affect Waterfront Property Values: Evidence from a Regulated Lake System
detail.abstract: Climate change is increasing hydrologic variability and management trade-offs. This study examines how managed lake-level fluctuations are capitalized into waterfront property values within a regulated lake system in Wisconsin, USA. By linking residential property transactions from 2013-2024 with high-frequency hydrologic and lake water-quality data, we estimate two-way fixed-effects hedonic models that isolate the economic impacts of deviations from expected seasonal lake levels under existing management rules. The results indicate that seasonal lake-level deviations (in.) reduce waterfront property sale prices by about 2 percent. Additional functional-form analyses provide limited evidence of strong nonlinear or asymmetric responses. Monte Carlo simulations suggest that stabilizing seasonal lake-level deviations within ±3 inches increase the aggregate value of lakefront housing by approximately $4.6 million (2013 USD), equivalent to an average gain of roughly $16,254 per property. The findings demonstrate how housing markets internalize hydrologic instability in regulated freshwater systems facing increasing climate risk.

title: TIPS under FIRE - Formation of Inflation Expectations in Bond Markets
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) - Institute for Finance and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) - Institute for Finance

detail.title: TIPS under FIRE - Formation of Inflation Expectations in Bond Markets
detail.abstract: We study the formation of inflation expectations in treasury bond markets along the termstructure. Our results point to deviations from the full-information rational expectation (FIRE) model by the marginal investor. Market expectations overreact to inflation news and this overreaction becomes more pronounced at longer horizons. We show that these results are both theoretically as well as empirically extremely difficult to reconcile with an alternative explanation by time-varying risk premia. The non-FIRE inflation expectations we document offer an explanation for the puzzling excess-volatility and excess-news-sensitivity of long-term yields.

title: The Verification Paradox

detail.title: The Verification Paradox
detail.abstract: When a student uses generative AI to produce academic work, the capacity to verify that work fails for two parties, for two reasons, at two moments. The teacher, examining the finished artifact, cannot determine who performed the thinking. The student, situated inside the process of production, cannot determine whether the material the system has supplied is correct, deep, or safe to build upon. This paper concerns the second failure. It argues that a student operating outside their own domain of competence faces three distinct verification problems-correctness, depth, and calibration-and that the third is the most consequential, because it is not a failure to check but a failure to recognize that anything requires checking. The paper then argues that this predicament is not reducible to the familiar condition of novice ignorance. AI-sourced claims differ structurally from textbook-sourced claims in a way that is independent of quality: no accountable party stands behind any particular sentence, which removes the external correction mechanism that has historically made novice learning survivable. Following recent work on the testimony gap, the paper shows this difference to be structural rather than incidental, and therefore permanent: it does not resolve as the underlying systems improve. Finally, the paper argues that the most natural institutional response-verifying student understanding through oral defense-cannot close the gap, because ownership and validity are independent variables. A student can genuinely own a false claim. Any instrument that certifies ownership while remaining blind to validity does not merely fail to detect the problem; it launders it, converting an unverified claim into credentialed knowledge.

title: Differentiated Integration in EU External Security Governance: The Case of Security and Defence Partnerships in Comparative Perspective
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Differentiated Integration in EU External Security Governance: The Case of Security and Defence Partnerships in Comparative Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or any data requiring ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This article analyses the European Union's Security and Defence Partnerships (SDPs) signed with twelve countries between 2024 and 2026 through the lens of Differentiated Integration theory. Using comparative content analysis with discourse-sensitive coding, the study reveals that these partnerships are shaped not by candidate status but by strategic alignment, political trust and institutional capacity. The central argument is that the EU has transformed its enlargement-based instrument into a selective, multi-layered security network, producing a five-tier structure of differentiation in its external security governance. The findings show that while the SDPs synthesise Neo-Realist concerns over power diversification and Liberal Institutionalism's emphasis on institutional cooperation, their legally non-binding nature constitutes a significant weakness. The article contributes to the literature on external differentiated integration by demonstrating how the EU's internal integration logic is transferred to external security policy. It offers policy recommendations: enhancing legal bindingness through financial instruments like SAFE; tiered access to EU funding; institutionalised monitoring mechanisms; balancing capacity-building with equal partnership for Global South states; and managing internal EU divergence on selectivity. The article concludes that the SDPs are an intermediate, hybrid instrument-neither a substitute for enlargement nor a replacement for traditional partnerships, but a new category of institutionalised flexibility.

title: When the Anchor Doesn't Move: Dollar Invoicing and the Limits of Partner-Currency Pass-Through under Azerbaijan's Peg, 2006-2026
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: When the Anchor Doesn't Move: Dollar Invoicing and the Limits of Partner-Currency Pass-Through under Azerbaijan's Peg, 2006-2026
detail.abstract: A hard exchange-rate peg fixes one bilateral rate by policy while leaving every other bilateral rate free to move. This paper uses Azerbaijan's de facto U.S.-dollar peg (near AZN 1.70/USD since 2017) as an identification device to ask how much of a trading partner's currency movement reaches domestic consumer prices when the dollar leg is frozen. Using 245 monthly observations (2006-2026), official central-bank nominal bilateral rates validated against an independent triangulated series, and Jordà local projections, we separate a common dollar cycle from idiosyncratic partner-currency shocks. Three findings survive rigorous inference. First, idiosyncratic partner-currency swings-movements orthogonal to the dollar cycle-do not reliably reach consumer prices (wild-bootstrap bands include zero at all horizons), consistent with dominant-currency (dollar) invoicing insulating the economy from partner-specific volatility. Second, the economy is nonetheless not broadly insulated: aggregate effective-rate pass-through reaches roughly 0.30 at twelve months, near the lower bound of the import-content benchmark, so broad manat movements-such as the 2015 devaluations-transmit substantially. Third, partnercurrency transmission appears mainly in acute crisis episodes (the 2018 lira crisis; the 2022 ruble collapse-and-surge), and an apparent asymmetry between imported inflation and disinflation is specific to the 2022 sanctions episode rather than a structural feature of the peg. The results imply that under the peg the central bank need not lean against ordinary partner-currency volatility, but that the peg's own credibility-and dollar invoicing-carry the burden of insulation.

title: The Schedule Elasticity of Demand in Project-based Retail Categories

detail.title: The Schedule Elasticity of Demand in Project-based Retail Categories
detail.abstract: Retail promotion research has established that price discounts accelerate purchases, with a substantial share of the promotional sales bump attributable to purchases shifted across time (van Heerde, Leeflang and Wittink 2004). This paper proposes a boundary condition on that mechanism: temporal shifting requires that the consumer controls purchase timing. In project-based categories, where the purchase is embedded in a sequenced undertaking involving third parties, timing is governed by the project schedule rather than the promotional calendar. I term the resulting demand behavior schedule elasticity and distinguish it from price elasticity: schedule-elastic demand may be price-sensitive in vendor selection yet price-insensitive in transaction timing. The framework yields three testable predictions: promotional lift declines as sequencing dependency rises; post-promotion troughs attenuate, because demand that cannot be pulled forward leaves no deficit behind; and the composition of remaining response shifts from acceleration toward switching. Descriptive evidence from a 2026 US sales event is consistent with the first prediction: within a single room category, standalone kitchen goods lifted 75 percent against baseline while installed kitchen fixtures lifted 35 percent. The paper situates the mechanism within current 1 housing-market conditions, where mortgage rate lock-in (Batzer, Coste, Doerner and Seiler 2024) is shifting demand composition toward project-embedded replacement purchases, and discusses implications for promotion measurement, event KPI design and demand forecasting in home improvement retail.

title: From Prediction to Decision: An Operational Audit Framework for AI Driven Lending, Based on Traditional Banking Controls

detail.title: From Prediction to Decision: An Operational Audit Framework for AI Driven Lending, Based on Traditional Banking Controls

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or sensitive personal data and does not require ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: AI models are now taking lending decisions that were earlier taken by bank officers. Credit scoring, loan approval and recovery prioritisation are increasingly automated, especially in digital lending. Regulators have responded at the policy level. The Reserve Bank of India has issued Digital Lending Directions in 2025 and draft guidance on model risk management that covers artificial intelligence and machine learning models. However, these frameworks mainly set expectations at the board and policy level. There is limited practical guidance on what oversight of AI lending decisions should look like at the operational level, in daily work. This paper addresses that gap. Drawing on the author's experience of managing 2,500 to 3,000 loan accounts and supporting reporting across 27 branches in a regional rural bank, the paper identifies four traditional banking controls that kept human lending decisions accountable: sanctioning authority chains, credit red flag checks, early warning monitoring of overdue accounts, and maker checker review. It then translates each control into an equivalent operational control for AI lending systems. The paper argues that effective AI oversight in lending does not require inventing new tools. It requires translating controls that banks already understand into the AI context, in a form that small NBFCs and fintech lenders can actually implement. The paper also outlines an open toolkit of templates based on this framework. This extends the author's earlier work on decision centric analytics, which found that systems influence outcomes only when they are integrated into daily decision making.

title:
A Green Energy Economy 

Legal Aspects and the Role of Environmental Economics
affiliations: NATIONAL KAPODISTRIAN UNIVERSITY OF ATHENS

detail.title:
A Green Energy Economy 

Legal Aspects and the Role of Environmental Economics
detail.abstract: The transition to a green energy economy is not a discrete programme of energy substitution. It is a reallocation of capital, risk, rights and public authority across the entire economy. Law determines which environmental costs enter market prices, who may build and connect clean infrastructure, how scarcity rents are distributed, which claims count as sustainable finance and how losses are shared among workers, consumers, investors and regions. Environmental economics supplies the analytical tools for those choices, but it does not itself resolve questions of legitimacy, distribution or rights. This study develops an integrated legal and economic account of the transition, centred on international climate law and European Union law and supported by comparative case law. It argues that effective legal design requires a coordinated policy mix: binding carbon budgets, credible carbon pricing, technology-neutral competition where feasible, targeted public support where market failures persist, accelerated but rights-compliant permitting, infrastructure regulation, truthful sustainability disclosure and compensatory social policy. It also identifies the limits of price signals where information, network, innovation, capital-market and political failures interact. The governing standard is therefore not maximum decarbonisation at any cost, but cost-effective decarbonisation within constitutional, environmental and social constraints.

title: Determinants of Airline Profitability: An Empirical Study on Ethiopian Airlines (2004-2024)

detail.title: Determinants of Airline Profitability: An Empirical Study on Ethiopian Airlines (2004-2024)
detail.abstract:
This study examines the determinants of Ethiopian Airlines' profitability using annual data from 2004/05 to 2023/24. Over this period, the airline expanded its fleet from 25 to 154 aircraft and increased revenue from approximately US$0.5 billion to over US$7 billion. The study investigates whether profitability is associated with operational efficiency, fleet expansion, and macroeconomic factors.

The analysis addresses two major econometric challenges. First, several variables exhibit strong upward trends, generating severe multicollinearity. A parsimonious specification using fleet size and load factor reduces the mean VIF from 58.34 to approximately 1. Second, the residuals exhibit substantial serial correlation (Durbin–Watson = 0.46; Breusch–Godfrey p = 0.0002). Newey–West standard errors and Prais–Winsten estimation are used as robustness corrections.

The results show that fleet size has the strongest association with profitability in levels models. Each additional aircraft is associated with approximately US$6.5 million higher annual net profit. However, this relationship disappears in first-difference estimation, suggesting that the association reflects long-run organizational scaling rather than a short-run mechanical return from adding aircraft. The findings are consistent with a model in which network expansion, capability accumulation, and market development generate profitability over time.

Exchange-rate movements are also positively associated with profit per aircraft, consistent with Ethiopian Airlines' substantial foreign-currency revenue base. Load factor is not statistically significant, likely reflecting limited variation over the sample period.

The study is limited by its single-airline design and small sample size. The results should therefore be interpreted as evidence of long-run association rather than causal effects.

title: United States Financial Sanctions and the Surge of Chinese Lending
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Department of Economics, University of Macau, University of Macau and

detail.title: United States Financial Sanctions and the Surge of Chinese Lending
detail.abstract: Do U.S. financial sanctions enable China to gain global influence? Using deal-level syndicated loan data, this study shows that these sanctions led to almost a 30% reduction in western credit to firms in sanctioned countries that Chinese banks in the Mainland, G7 and Financial Centers offset by 7.3%, 0.7% and 5.1%, respectively. The estimates are conservative and robust to a correction for bank-branch selection and controls for trade sanctions. In sanctioned countries, Chinese banks made loans primarily to repeat borrowers, and Chinese lenders responded more aggressively to joint G7 versus unilateral U.S. financial sanctions.

title: Modeling Inflation, Public Debt, and Exchange Rate Dynamics in Small Open Economies: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Synthesis
affiliations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development. Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training den Entrepreneurial Development,, University of Bradford and Transilvania University of Brasov

detail.title: Modeling Inflation, Public Debt, and Exchange Rate Dynamics in Small Open Economies: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Synthesis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Introduction: Small open economies struggle to simultaneously control inflation, manage public debt, and stabilize foreign exchange rates. Although researchers have deployed diverse econometric toolkits to model this macroeconomic nexus, the applied literature remains methodologically fragmented, lacking a systematic synthesis of model choices, geographic focus, and reporting quality.

Methods: This systematic review executed a PRISMA-guided Python 3,12 script to search for studies across OpenAlex, CrossRef, and Semantic Scholar (1970–2026). This was supplemented with a manual search to retrieve studies indexed in Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar. Screening 1,122 raw records through a quota-balanced sampling protocol yielded a synthesized corpus of 120 studies across eight econometric families. The corpus was categorized geographically into Ghana-anchored (38.3%), Sub-Saharan Africa/small open economies (36.7%), foundational methodological (18.3%), and other emerging markets (6.7%). Automated full-text text-mining proxies assessed reporting transparency, while a citation-velocity funnel regression evaluated visibility asymmetry.

Results: Autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL/NARDL) bounds-testing is the most prevalent primary model family (18.3%), followed by DSGE/NKPC (13.3%) and ECM/VECM (12.5%), with a notable post-2017 shift toward asymmetric and time-varying specifications. Full-text transparency varies sharply: only 6.2% of DSGE studies explicitly state a sample period, compared to 52.0% of ARDL studies, and fewer than 30% of studies in any family report explicit diagnostic checks. A statistically significant citation funnel asymmetry (Egger-style slope = −1.27, p = 0.005) reveals that older, foundational methodological papers receive disproportionate citation visibility over recent regional applied studies.

Discussion: The field lacks a standardized evidence base. Reduced-form ARDL/NARDL and ECM/VECM frameworks offer the most immediate baseline for future quantitative meta-analyses. Finally, this review delivers a data-driven decision framework to guide model selection in small open economies.

title: International Security & Geopolitics Working Paper Series

detail.title: International Security & Geopolitics Working Paper Series

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, animals, interviews, surveys, experiments, or the collection of personal data. It is based on conceptual, comparative, and secondary-source analysis. Therefore, ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Traditional conceptualizations of sovereignty in international relations—predominantly rooted in Westphalian autonomy and classical realism—remain limited in their ability to explain subtle, non-kinetic, and institutionally mediated forms of contemporary influence. While classical colonialism and mandate systems relied on physical occupation and formal administrative control, and while neo-colonialism emphasized economic extraction, the twenty-first century has generated more complex patterns of sovereignty erosion. This paper introduces Modern Mandate Theory (MMT) as an analytical framework for examining how major external actors may constrain the effective decision-making capacity of formally independent states without necessarily altering their legal borders or relying primarily on overt kinetic force. The paper argues that such processes may operate through institutional penetration, digital and data dependency, elite realignment, and the gradual weakening of strategic administrative cadres. Modern Mandate Theory argues that in the twenty-first century, sovereignty can be eroded not necessarily through formal occupation, colonial administration, or legal annexation, but through externally structured systems of dependency, institutional penetration, technological reliance, elite alignment, cognitive-political conditioning, and constrained decision-making autonomy. To operationalize these concepts, the study constructs the National Resilience Index (NRI)—a composite diagnostic framework that assesses resilience in sovereignty across nine dimensions: historical memory, institutional resilience, strategic culture, educational sovereignty, technological competence, social cohesion, economic autonomy, data sovereignty, and decision-making independence. By applying MMT and the NRI to sixteen comparative case studies—Finland, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Japan, Kazakhstan, Moldova, North Korea, Poland, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Korea, Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan—this working paper suggests that sovereignty may be understood not only as a binary legal status, but also as a variable condition shaped by institutional autonomy, strategic capacity, and external dependency. The framework contributes to the literature by shifting attention from kinetic indicators of hybrid warfare toward the institutional foundations of sovereign decision-making autonomy.

title: Aggregate Optimality Does Not Imply Functional Efficiency: A Reinterpretation of the Triffin Dilemma

detail.title: Aggregate Optimality Does Not Imply Functional Efficiency: A Reinterpretation of the Triffin Dilemma
detail.abstract:
Sovereign debt is typically evaluated in aggregate, with sustainability inferred from its size, financing cost, and market demand. This note argues that such evaluations may be fundamentally incomplete because a single observable debt stock can simultaneously support multiple economically distinct functions. Specifically, U.S. Treasury liabilities embed a fundamental financing function and a distance-induced coordination function, yet both are priced through one common market yield.
The central analytical result is that aggregate optimality does not imply function specific efficiency. When multiple functions are bundled within one observable instrument, aggregate marginal equality can coexist with persistent marginal inefficiencies across the underlying functions. Expansion may therefore continue even after one function has exceeded its efficient level, because pricing reflects aggregate rather than function-specific conditions. The framework provides a functional reinterpretation of the Triffin dilemma. Exorbitant Privilege arises from the global demand for the coordination services embedded in U.S. Treasury securities, while Exorbitant Burden reflects the growing costs associated with the fundamental financing function. As long as the former offsets the latter, aggregate debt may continue to appear sustainable despite the gradual accumulation of hidden functional misallocation. Debt crises may therefore emerge not from excessive debt alone, but from the eventual revelation of inefficiencies concealed within an aggregated liability structure.

title: Belief Records and the Price of Disaster Fear
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC)

detail.title: Belief Records and the Price of Disaster Fear
detail.abstract: In a complete-market economy in which investors hold a disaster model until its sinceadoption record rejects it, the equilibrium risk-neutral disaster intensity factors exactly into a representative-agent benchmark times a wealth-weighted power mean of current beliefs. Inversion recovers the market's priced disaster belief, not the physical law. However, that belief aggregate is not the complete pricing state: continuation values depend on the law governing belief revision, and that law depends on the records under which current beliefs have survived. Therefore, conditional on the current option state, proxies for those survival records forecast the slope of the disaster-tail term structure-a residual that belief-sufficient models set to zero.

title: Agricultural Trade Policy and Water Quality: Evidence from the Mexican Hass Avocado Import Program
affiliations: and

detail.title: Agricultural Trade Policy and Water Quality: Evidence from the Mexican Hass Avocado Import Program
detail.abstract: The 2016 Mexican Hass Avocado Import Program opened the U.S. market to fresh Hass avocados from all of Mexico, conditional on individual states meeting strict phytosanitary requirements. We provide hydrology-based empirical evidence that the 2016 program led to improvements in Mexico's surface water quality. Our differencein-differences estimates illustrate improvements of 12 percent in biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), 11 percent in chemical oxygen demand (COD), and 10 percent in nitrogen concentrations. We argue that the program encouraged farmers to adopt cleaner production methods with lower pesticide and fertilizer applications that, in turn, resulted in these water quality gains.

title: The Regulatory Divergence and Risk Analysis of Cross-Border M&A: A Case Study of Microsoft's Acquisition of Activision Blizzard

detail.title: The Regulatory Divergence and Risk Analysis of Cross-Border M&A: A Case Study of Microsoft's Acquisition of Activision Blizzard
detail.abstract: With the intensification of global technology competition, cross-border mergers and acquisitions (M&A), increasingly face fragmented antitrust review across multiple jurisdictions. This paper examines Microsoft Corporation's $68.7 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard, Inc. as a case study of how divergent regulatory philosophies among leading competition authorities can reshape a single transaction. Combining doctrinal legal analysis with a chronological case study, the paper traces the deal's transaction structure and the parallel merger reviews conducted by the European Commission, the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), and the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), together with the eventual restructuring of the transaction to secure clearance. The analysis finds that although the three authorities examined substantially the same evidence, they reached materially different conclusions on remedy adequacy: the European Commission accepted behavioral licensing commitments, the CMA required a structural divestiture, and the FTC's litigation failed in federal court. The paper further evaluates the deal's risk allocation mechanisms including a $3 billion reverse termination fee and its post-closing compliance obligations. The findings suggest that in contemporary cross-border M&A, the most restrictive regulator, rather than the most permissive, determines the final deal architecture.

title: Faithful Intelligence Theory: Explaining Human-AI Pedagogical Collaboration for Leadership Formation and Learning
affiliations: Liberty University

detail.title: Faithful Intelligence Theory: Explaining Human-AI Pedagogical Collaboration for Leadership Formation and Learning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or non-financial conflicts of interest related to this conceptual manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual and theoretical study did not involve human participants, human-participant data, or identifiable personal information. Institutional review board approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external grant funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This manuscript presents Faithful Intelligence Theory, a middle-range educational theory that proposes an explanation of how guided human–AI pedagogical collaboration may transform leadership learning into leadership formation. In this usage, faithful denotes fidelity to evidence, educational purpose, ethical commitments, professional responsibility, and human dignity; in Christian settings, the term may also carry theological meaning. The theory's central mechanism, Guided Reflective Verification, is proposed to explain how AI-supported learning may cultivate judgment, ethical reasoning, wisdom, and responsible agency rather than merely accelerating task completion. The manuscript develops the theory's constitutional vocabulary, formal foundations, six principal propositions (with Proposition 5 divided into moderation and recursive-development functions), the Faithful Intelligence Framework, and the eight-stage Human–AI Learning Cycle, and it proposes a research infrastructure for future empirical validation. The theory is offered as a conceptual contribution; its propositions have not yet been tested empirically. As the foundational paper for the Faithful Intelligence Research Program, this manuscript provides the governing theoretical architecture for earlier working papers on epistemic governance and theological governance in interreligious religious education, while establishing the basis for future theological, educational, measurement, engineering, organizational, sector-specific, and theory-development studies.

title: Reward-Free Reinforcement Learning Before Knowing What Will Matter

detail.title: Reward-Free Reinforcement Learning Before Knowing What Will Matter
detail.abstract: Economic diagnosis often begins before its eventual objective is known. This paper studies a reward-free information contract in which controlled transition data are collected at that earlier date, frozen, and reused after one or more objectives are disclosed. A regulator chooses between collecting broadly now and waiting to target data after the diagnostic margin is known. Suppose tasks arrive at rate 𝜆, the transition law expires at rate 𝛿, and margin 𝑗 must meet root mean squared error tolerance 𝜀 𝑗. Collecting before disclosure is optimal exactly when the expected number of tasks before expiration, 𝜆/𝛿, exceeds a precision-weighted task-diversity threshold. With quadratic diagnostic loss, the optimal allocation places more observations on noisy, valuable, and more likely margins. A designed repeated-response economy then shows the continuation value preserved by a frozen model. Against the same exact-policy benchmark, sequential planning loses 0.0003 units of expected value in the assurance task, compared with 0.0919 for the one-step rule at the registered cost. The difference vanishes at the calibration boundary. Passive histories and institutional records delimit the certificate by showing which deviations are observed and feasible.

title: The Cost of Early Access
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: The Cost of Early Access
detail.abstract: Using new data, we document a previously unstudied feature of financial services recruiting: at least 50 major firms operate a parallel hiring market eight months before the standard cycle that recruits candidates from underrepresented demographic groups. We offer an economic explanation for how diversity-conscious recruiting can alter not only who is hired but also the timing of hiring. Since demographic characteristics are observable ex-ante, firms that value representation gain less from waiting for additional information about candidate quality. Exploiting the staggered adoption of early recruitment programs across firms, we find evidence consistent with the model's prediction of reduced match quality, although we cannot distinguish compositional changes from information effects. After program adoption, the share of interns in a cohort who study at universities without established on-campus recruiting pipelines increases by 16.5 percentage points, while demographic composition remains unchanged. Interns from these schools become 13 percentage points less likely to return to the firm after their internship and 23 percentage points less likely to remain there two years later.

title: Capable Artificial Intelligence, Vulnerable Users

detail.title: Capable Artificial Intelligence, Vulnerable Users

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and Principal Investigator of Aero Shield UAS Services, LLC. The framework developed in this paper originated in prior work on supervisory control for autonomous safety-critical systems conducted in that context. This research received no external funding, and the author has no financial interest in any of the companies, products, or litigation discussed. The author has no other interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This work is a conceptual analysis involving no human participants or primary data collection. The illustrative scenes are constructed composites, not case studies of identifiable individuals, and the documented cases discussed are drawn from public court filings and Congressional testimony.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Consumer artificial intelligence now engages people continuously in the ordinary settings of their lives: in their homes, their workplaces, their clinics, and their private conversations. The framework currently called algorithmic accountability was built for a narrower problem, the discrete consequential decision an institution makes about a person in credit, employment, housing, or healthcare. It was not built for systems that engage a person continuously, and it does not reach the harms that engagement produces. This paper extends that framework into the domain where consumer AI actually operates. It works through four scenes from everyday life, identifies the structural pattern they share, and shows that the pattern is not new: it is the paradox of automation that Lisanne Bainbridge named in 1983, now operating on ordinary users rather than trained professionals. The argument is anchored in a real case, the death of a sixteen-year-old whose months of conversation with a consumer chatbot are the subject of sworn Congressional testimony and active litigation. The paper grounds its response in the way earlier capable technologies were brought under governance, in seatbelts, aviation, nuclear power, and pharmaceuticals, and develops five algorithmic accountability properties that consumer AI systems should be required to have. The argument is offered on operational and structural grounds. It does not depend on any claim about whether these systems have minds of their own.

title: Asymmetric Hedging: How South Asian States Exploit Sino-Indian Financial Rivalry

detail.title: Asymmetric Hedging: How South Asian States Exploit Sino-Indian Financial Rivalry
detail.abstract: This paper examines the international political economy of competitive development finance between China and India in South Asia, with particular reference to Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and Nepal. Departing from narratives that emphasise Creditor-driven influence, this study introduces the concept of Asymmetric Hedging to explain how smaller South Asian states actively navigate structural differences between competing bilateral financing architectures to preserve domestic policy autonomy and manage sovereign risk. Building on Susan Strange's theory of Structural Finance Power and extending the small-state hedging literature associated with Cheng-Chwee Kuik, the paper employs a comparative case-study methodology with structured process tracing, examining the cases of Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and Nepal. The empirical record across all three cases indicates that Colombo, Dhaka, and Kathmandu have each, in structurally distinct ways, converted Sino-Indian financial rivalry into enhanced bargaining leverage vis-à-vis both creditors. In Sri Lanka, asymmetric hedging was evident when, amid the 2022 sovereign default, the country simultaneously secured emergency financial support from both New Delhi and Beijing, at a time when neither major power could risk appearing disengaged from a strategically significant neighbor. In Bangladesh, Asymmetric Hedging can be seen in the strategic management of financing commitments from both India and China, where disbursements are carefully balanced to maintain policy autonomy and avoid long term dependency on either of the two. In Nepal, Asymmetric Hedging is demonstrated through their persistent requests for Grants rather than loans from China's BRI, while at the same time deepening hydropower collaboration with India, hence balancing the influence from both sides. These findings indicate that structural finance power in a competitive geoeconomic environment is neither linear nor unidirectional.The rivalry between creditors inherently reduces their leverage, as recipient states use that competition to their advantage. The paper concludes by discussing implications for development finance theory and the future of South Asian geoeconomics.

title: A Review of Financial Integration: Focus on the Divergence in Measurement Methods
affiliations: University of London - International Programmes

detail.title: A Review of Financial Integration: Focus on the Divergence in Measurement Methods
detail.abstract: Financial Integration (FI) measurement remains disputed as a subject, with several methods rendering different estimations on the state of FI across international equity markets. This paper sought to review the shortcomings evidenced by literature which range from data selection, parameters to model specification. Every metric used as proxy of FI and the tests done to determine validity and reliability are discussed in a methodological review. An application of dynamic copula modelling derived from a study in the review provides an estimation of the levels of Financial Integration of developing equity markets at country level on a yearly basis between 2003 and 2023 benchmarked to developed markets.

title: Climate Smart Agroforestry for Restoration of Degraded Peatlands and Contribution to Climate and Livelihood Goals in South Sumatra
affiliations: Center for International Forestry Research, CIFOR-ICRAF, CIFOR-ICRAF, affiliation not provided to SSRN, CIFOR-ICRAF, Ayer Rajah Crescent , CIFOR-ICRAF, BRIN and CIFOR-ICRAF

detail.title: Climate Smart Agroforestry for Restoration of Degraded Peatlands and Contribution to Climate and Livelihood Goals in South Sumatra
detail.abstract: South Sumatra has a large area of peatlands (i.e. 1.06 to 1.5 million ha, based on the mapping methodology), and much of these peatlands are converted to other land uses, made it more vulnerable to fire. This area is therefore, one of the nation’s important peatland restoration targets. The main objective of this paper is to review various agroforestry systems exist in the peatlands in Indonesia, and based on that, identify potential agroforestry models suitable to practice in South Sumatra’s peatland area. Reviewed data were then analyzed through narrative qualitative and narrative comparative methods with careful compilation and scientific interpretation. There are various agroforestry systems exist in the Indonesian peatlands providing multiple ecosystem benefits to local and wider scale. However, considering potential benefits for the peatlands in South Sumatra, i.e. restoration, biodiversity conservation, diversifying farm production, and socioeconomic benefits, our suggested agroforestry models are the combination of various trees, with understory crops, fishery and honey. Besides various benefits provided by agroforestry, including its strong roles achieving nine out of seventeen sustainable development goals (SDGs), further investigation from crop ecophysiology to market mechanisms, will be required for wider agroforestry adoption.

title: Disagreement on Volatility
affiliations: Shenzhen University

detail.title: Disagreement on Volatility
detail.abstract: We study how disagreement about future risk shapes stock prices. Guided by a two-dimensional belief framework distinguishing risk disagreement from return disagreement, we construct a machine-learning-based stock-level measure of disagreement about future return volatility (DOV). DOV negatively predicts subsequent stock returns in the cross section and retains incremental predictive power beyond established measures of return disagreement. Consistent with the portfolio-demand mechanism, high-DOV stocks have lower institutional ownership, experience subsequent reductions in institutional holdings, and exhibit lower future trading activity. The negative DOV-return relation is stronger for firms with greater valuation uncertainty and more severe limits to arbitrage. A bottom-up aggregate of stock-level DOV also negatively predicts future market returns. Our findings identify heterogeneous risk beliefs as a distinct second dimension of investor disagreement and highlight their implications for portfolio allocation, market participation, and asset pricing.

title: Do Carbon Price Forecasts Improve Compliance Procurement? Evidence from European Union Allowances
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Center for Forecasting Science; Academy of Mathematics and Systems Sciences and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Do Carbon Price Forecasts Improve Compliance Procurement? Evidence from European Union Allowances
detail.abstract: Firms covered by emissions trading systems need forecasts not only to value allowances, but also to decide when to buy them. This paper asks whether European Union Allowance (EUA) prices contain short-horizon predictability that survives a forecast-origin information design and improves simulated compliance procurement. Using daily data from 2019 to 2025, we produce direct forecasts for one to five trading days ahead. All predictors are observable at the forecast origin, and calibration and model-selection rules are fixed before the final holdout. The released forecast has the lowest point-estimate RMSE at every horizon among fourteen benchmarks, with the strongest loss-difference evidence at horizons three and four. Relative to a random walk, out-of-sample R-squared rises from 1.2% at one day to 15.5% at five days. We then use the forecast path in a constrained procurement problem with execution costs, market impact, capacity limits, and tail risk; sensitivity exercises add demand uncertainty. For a fixed 100,000-EUA order, optimized schedules lower average realized costs by 8.5 to 38.5 basis points relative to uniform execution across horizons h = 2 to h = 5. The gains come from reallocating purchases within a fixed window, not from reliable next-day directional timing.

title: Greening the Bottom Line: Natural Capital’s Role in Mitigating Carbon Inequality
affiliations: University of Queensland, Beijing Institute of Petrochemical Technology, Independent, Montpellier Business School- Energy and Sustainable Development and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Greening the Bottom Line: Natural Capital’s Role in Mitigating Carbon Inequality
detail.abstract: Carbon inequality is increasingly recognized as a significant issue that requires attention to ensure an equitable and sustainable climate transition. Although previous studies have extensively examined factors such as income, consumption, and energy in determining carbon inequality, less work has examined the role of natural capital in this process. This study aims to examine the effect of natural capital on carbon inequality in Australia from 1995 to 2024, while accounting for the roles of economic globalization, financial development, economic growth, and the private sector. For this reason, the structural break unit root test, the structural break ARDL bounds test, and the dynamic ARDL simulation technique are employed to analyse the study variables’ long- and short-run properties. From our findings, there exists long-run relationship between the variables. Natural capital is negatively associated with carbon inequality, whereas economic globalization, financial development, and economic growth are positively associated with it. In contrast, private-sector activity is found to reduce carbon inequality. Additionally, our non-linear regression model suggests that natural capital and carbon inequality have an inverted-U relationship, implying that the negative effects of natural capital on carbon inequality intensify with the maturity of natural capital. On the other hand, a U-shaped relationship exists between economic globalization and carbon inequality, implying that the positive effects of economic globalization diminish as globalization increases environmental disparity. Our study makes important contributions to the literature by shifting the perspective on the roles of natural capital in promoting carbon neutrality and reducing carbon inequality. Our results indicate that restoring the ecosystem, promoting biodiversity, and adopting effective natural resource management policies would improve both carbon inequality and carbon emissions.

title: Should Renewable Curtailment Be Treated as a Planning Risk?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Texas A&M University and Teesside University

detail.title: Should Renewable Curtailment Be Treated as a Planning Risk?
detail.abstract: Renewable curtailment is becoming increasingly common in power systems with high renewable penetration, yet it is often treated as an operational inefficiency rather than a planning risk. This paper develops a decision-dependent framework to evaluate how renewable expansion and siting decisions shape curtailment outcomes under uncertainty. The framework combines a two-stage stochastic capacity expansion model with an ex post curtailment risk assessment based on expected value and Conditional Value-at-Risk, where curtailment arises endogenously from network-constrained dispatch decisions. It evaluates three complementary risk measures: revenue loss risk, curtailment cost risk, and siting-induced curtailment risk, and employs a structured sensitivity-interaction approximation approach to enable tractable evaluation of alternative renewable portfolios. The approach is applied to the 2030 New York State power system, a renewable-rich and transmission-constrained system with persistent spatial mismatches between generation and demand. The results show that curtailment risk is highly location-dependent, with a small number of zones carrying a disproportionately large share of curtailment risk. Wind exhibits steeper and more system-wide risk escalation than solar, with larger spillovers and greater dependence on penetration level, whereas solar curtailment remains more spatially contained. The analysis further shows that curtailment is strongly tail-sensitive, meaning that adverse weather scenarios can produce much larger losses than average outcomes suggest. These tail-risk effects, particularly for wind and high-penetration cases, indicate that reliance on average curtailment alone is insufficient for evaluating renewable siting decisions and for informing transmission and flexibility planning.

title: From Division to Cohesion: A New Vision for the NFC Awards to Strengthen Political-Economic-Social Union and Common Citizenship in Pakistan
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE)

detail.title: From Division to Cohesion: A New Vision for the NFC Awards to Strengthen Political-Economic-Social Union and Common Citizenship in Pakistan
detail.abstract: This paper critiques Pakistan's current National Finance Commission (NFC) Award system and proposes a transformative vision for intergovernmental fiscal transfers. While the existing “gap-filling” approach provides some stability and predictable financing, it is criticized as a “pragmatic yet unscientific” method that uses arbitrary weights, disincentivizes provincial revenue collection, and fails to address horizontal fiscal inequities. The paper proposes a formal fiscal equalization program designed to ensure that all Pakistani citizens—including those in the provisional provinces and the capital—receive comparable public services at comparable tax burdens. The proposed system consists of two primary pillars: (a) Fiscal Capacity Equalization, which utilizes provincial GDP as a macro-indicator to bring fiscally disadvantaged provinces up to a national average per capita fiscal capacity; and (b) Fiscal Need Equalization, which employs the Demand for Public Services (DPS) approach, allocating funds based on objective demand-side indicators (e.g., school-age population for education, road kilometers for transportation) rather than supply-side costs. The paper concludes that moving to a transparent, objective, formula-based fiscal equalization system will foster an internal common market, encourage labour and capital mobility, and strengthen the political-economic-social union of Pakistan by ensuring regional fiscal equity and common citizenship.

title: Spillovers Across Blue Economy and Fossil Fuel Markets: A Quantile Time-Frequency Connectedness and Portfolio Perspective
affiliations: Charles University in Prague - Institute of Economic Studies, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Pir Mehr Ali Shah Arid Agriculture University Rawalpindi (PMAS), affiliation not provided to SSRN and York University - Schulich School of Business

detail.title: Spillovers Across Blue Economy and Fossil Fuel Markets: A Quantile Time-Frequency Connectedness and Portfolio Perspective
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of ocean-based industries and the growing financialization of blue economy assets have heightened investor interest in their exposure to energy-market risks and financial spillovers. This study examines the return connectedness between blue economy stocks and fossil energy assets using a quantile time-frequency connectedness framework over the period from October 2011 to October 2025. The findings reveal that connectedness is highly quantile-dependent, with spillovers intensifying substantially during extreme market conditions. Blue economy assets tend to transmit shocks in the short term under extreme market regimes but increasingly act as shock absorbers over medium- and long-term horizons. Moreover, the results show that short-term spillovers account for the largest share of connectedness, highlighting the dominant role of near-term energy-market shocks in shaping blue economy asset dynamics. Fossil energy assets generally emerge as net transmitters of risk, whereas blue economy assets primarily function as receivers, indicating that energy-market disturbances remain an important source of risk for ocean-related investments. These results highlight the regime-dependent risk-management benefits of connectedness-based portfolio strategies and provide actionable insights for investors, portfolio managers, and policymakers seeking to strengthen resilience to energy-market shocks in maritime-related financial markets.

title: Carbon Border Adjustment and the Design of Domestic Carbon Policy: A Structuralist Dynamic CGE Assessment for Tunisia
affiliations: Université de Poitiers

detail.title: Carbon Border Adjustment and the Design of Domestic Carbon Policy: A Structuralist Dynamic CGE Assessment for Tunisia
detail.abstract: The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) prices the carbon embodied in imported steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers and electricity, exposing developing exporters to a selective charge on the goods they sell to the Union. Using a dynamic, structuralist computable general equilibrium model of Tunisia---an economy in which saving and foreign exchange constrain growth and investment drives capital accumulation and productivity---we ask whether the country should absorb this charge or answer it with a carbon price of its own. After correcting each sector's exposure for the share genuinely covered and its European orientation, a passively borne CBAM lowers Tunisian GDP by about $0.5$ percent by 2035. The efficient response is a domestic carbon price levied on all covered production, whatever its destination, and credited against the CBAM at the border: charged on a far larger base than exports alone and recycled into public saving, it raises GDP to about 0.3 percent above baseline. This gain reflects higher investment financed by lower household consumption, not an improvement in welfare, and the price cuts emissions only where producers can abate. The ranking of policies is robust to how strongly saving translates into investment and to the model's key elasticities.

title: The Price of an Asset: Accounting, Framing, and the Political Economy of the $23.6 Trillion Decoupling Estimate

detail.title: The Price of an Asset: Accounting, Framing, and the Political Economy of the $23.6 Trillion Decoupling Estimate
detail.abstract: A widely reported EY-Parthenon estimate holds that reducing Western dependence on Chinese supply chains would require approximately $23.6 trillion in additional investment over twenty-five years. This paper does not dispute the magnitude of the estimate. It examines the accounting convention under which the figure is universally described-as a "cost"-and argues that this convention constitutes a category error with substantial policy consequences. The overwhelming majority of the estimated outlay funds durable capital assets (manufacturing, infrastructure, processing capacity, research facilities, and workforce formation) rather than consumed expenses; by the study's own sector breakdown, manufacturing, mining, and power and utilities alone account for nearly $13 trillion of the $23.6 trillion total. Treating capital formation as expense, rather than as investment yielding depreciable assets with multi-decade productive lives, systematically biases the estimate toward a conclusion of impossibility. The paper (i) develops the asset-versus-expense distinction and applies it to the estimate; (ii) restores the figure to scale, showing it represents roughly 1.8 percent of the three blocs' combined annual GDP; (iii) models the mechanism by which a proprietary, unverifiable number acquires the standing of consensus fact; (iv) identifies the one-sided structure of a decoupling model that prices Western adjustment while assigning Chinese adjustment a value of zero; and (v) concedes the genuine limits of the reframing-transition costs, inflationary drag, and duplicative capacity. The conclusion is not that decoupling is costless or advisable, but that the prevailing framing forecloses a debate the underlying arithmetic leaves open.

title: Uncertain Information Advantage and Price Discovery: Evidence from Data Vendor Dissemination Differences.
affiliations: INSEAD, Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business, London Business School and

detail.title: Uncertain Information Advantage and Price Discovery: Evidence from Data Vendor Dissemination Differences.
detail.abstract: Using intra-day trading data, we examine how uncertainty about the novelty of private information affects price discovery. Examining staggered and largely unpredictable disseminations of identical analyst forecasts by IBES and FactSet, we show that uncertainty about whether investors have already received and traded on the information, causes (i) stock prices to react at both disseminations, (ii) price discovery at the second release to decline with the time since the first release, and (iii) both price discovery and trade price impact at the second release to be negatively related to prior returns when those returns suggest earlier trading on the news.

title: Empirical Calibration and Validation of the Livelihood System Integrated Model (LSIM): Evidence from Multi-Sector Livelihood Shocks in Sierra Leone, 2004-2025
affiliations: Bank of Sierra Leone

detail.title: Empirical Calibration and Validation of the Livelihood System Integrated Model (LSIM): Evidence from Multi-Sector Livelihood Shocks in Sierra Leone, 2004-2025
detail.abstract: This study presents the first empirical application of the Livelihood Systems Integration Model (LSIM) developed by Jackson (2026) to examine how macroeconomic and sectoral shocks are transmitted through Sierra Leone's livelihood system over the period 2004-2025. The analysis calibrates the LSIM using annual macroeconomic, sectoral and livelihood data, estimates an LSIM-aligned recursive structural vector autoregression (SVAR) to evaluate the dynamic effects of mining and inflation shocks, and examines the relationship between poverty, vulnerable employment, agricultural employment, inflation and mining rents through a welfare equation. Impulse response analysis reveals that mineral-rent shocks stimulate short-term economic growth but generate only limited improvements in employment quality, reflecting weak domestic transmission from extractive activities. Inflation emerges as the most disruptive shock, reducing growth while increasing agricultural and vulnerable employment, thereby intensifying livelihood vulnerability. Remittances provide a modest counter-cyclical buffer but are insufficient to offset persistent structural weaknesses within the labour market. Although limited poverty observations constrain welfare estimation, the findings consistently say that inflation and vulnerable employment remain important channels through which macroeconomic instability influences household welfare. Robustness diagnostics confirm the stability of the estimated recursive SVAR and indicate no evidence of residual serial correlation, strengthening confidence in the empirical results. The study demonstrates that livelihoods are best understood as an interconnected system in which macroeconomic conditions, sectoral performance and household responses continually interact. It concludes that strengthening price stability, improving mining-sector linkages, investing in agricultural transformation, expanding adaptive social protection and enhancing livelihood data systems are essential for building resilience and reducing poverty, while establishing the LSIM as a practical framework for informing development policy in Sierra Leone and comparable resource-dependent economies.

title: Evaluating the Predictive Validity of ICT's Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution (AMD) Model on CME E-Mini NASDAQ-100 Futures

detail.title: Evaluating the Predictive Validity of ICT's Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution (AMD) Model on CME E-Mini NASDAQ-100 Futures

declarations.funderStatement: I funded the research.

detail.abstract: To our knowledge, this paper provides the first systematic quantitative evaluation of the ICT Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution (AMD) model on CME E-Mini NASDAQ-100 futures (NQ). The AMD model proposes that institutional participants structure intraday price delivery in three phases: overnight accumulation in the Asian session, a deliberate false breakout during London, and directional delivery to the opposing liquidity pool during the New York morning session. Using four years of real 15-minute OHLCV data from Databento (January 2022 to July 2026), we operationalize the AMD rules into a strict mechanical strategy and analyze the statistical properties of the resulting signal across N = 484 manipulation signal days using chi-square testing, Benjamini-Hochberg multiple comparisons correction, and regime-conditional analysis. Three principal findings emerge. First, the AMD manipulation signal fires on 44% of trading days. Second, 57% of valid signals see full target delivery before the 9:40 AM New York entry window opens, revealing a structural mismatch between the model's timing assumptions and actual price delivery. Third, within this operationalization of the AMD model, no directional information beyond the daily trend regime was observed: when the signal aligns with the trend it is correct 62–71% of the time (Cohen's h = 0.23–0.43); when it opposes the trend it is correct only 25–30% of the time (Cohen's h = 0.42–0.53). All four trending-regime cells survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Key findings are robust to variation in the manipulation breach threshold (5–20 NQ points), Asia range filter percentile, and stop buffer. The regime-dependent signal pattern constitutes a specific, testable hypothesis for follow-on research.

title: Real-Time Implementation Strategies for Frequency-Seletion Algorithms and Synthetic Radar Arrays Against B2 Bomber Threats: From Theory to Operational Deployment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Development Alternative and Jagannath University

detail.title: Real-Time Implementation Strategies for Frequency-Seletion Algorithms and Synthetic Radar Arrays Against B2 Bomber Threats: From Theory to Operational Deployment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest Statement: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The proliferation of advanced stealth platforms, such as the Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirit, necessitates an evolution in traditional air defense architectures beyond mere hardware upgrades. This paper investigates a novel dual-layered approach that first optimizes existing "normal" radars through intelligent frequency-seletion algorithms—specifically designed to identify and exploit gaps in the radar cross-section (RCS) characteristics of low-observable targets—and secondly, synthesizes a high-resolution detection network by fusing signals from distributed conventional sensors without physical retrofits. By dynamically selecting transmit frequencies based on real-time aspect-angle estimation and material absorption profiles, the proposed system maximizes return energy even against optimized stealth coatings. Furthermore, this study details the specific engineering steps required for real-life implementation, addressing latency constraints, synchronization protocols, data fusion architectures, and hardware integration challenges. The resulting architecture achieves robust detection probability while minimizing susceptibility to active electronically scanned array (AESA) jamming or internal resonance modes specific to the B-2's unique flying wing geometry.

title: Global citizenship education in southeast asia: A bibliometric analysis of research trends, collaboration networks, and knowledge gaps (2010-2025)
affiliations: Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Universitas Negeri Surabaya and Universitas Negeri Surabaya

detail.title: Global citizenship education in southeast asia: A bibliometric analysis of research trends, collaboration networks, and knowledge gaps (2010-2025)
detail.abstract: This study provides the first systematic bibliometric mapping of Global Citizenship Education (GCE) research in Southeast Asia, analyzing 764 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from the Scopus database spanning 2010 to 2025. Using Biblioshiny and VOSviewer, we conducted performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, intellectual leadership, dominant themes, collaboration networks, and critical knowledge gaps. Results reveal that GCE research in Southeast Asia has grown at an annual rate of 43.27%, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, with three distinct phases: embryonic (2010-2015), growth (2016-2019), and acceleration (2020-2025). The United States and Indonesia are the most productive countries, while Globalisation, Societies and Education leads among 388 journals. Thematic analysis reveals a predominant concentration in higher education contexts, with indigenous cultural values, local wisdom, and elementary education virtually absent from all nine keyword clusters. Country co-authorship network analysis reveals that, while individual intra-ASEAN ties such as Indonesia-Malaysia can be substantively strong, collaboration with Global North partners remains more extensive in aggregate. These findings provide researchers, educators, and policymakers with an evidence-based roadmap for advancing GCE in Southeast Asia, highlighting the urgent need for elementary-level research, integration of indigenous epistemologies, and development of regional research networks across ASEAN member states.

title: Research on BTC-Based Stablecoins
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Research on BTC-Based Stablecoins
detail.abstract: Starting from first principles, this paper systematically argues the theoretical selfconsistency and empirical foundation of a BTC-based, free-energy (joule)-anchored noncustodial stablecoin (J-ST). The full text merges four progressive studies into a complete research loop of "motivation → theory → design → empirics."

title: Developing an Integrated Bureaucratic Reform Model to Improve Public Healthcare Service Quality in Indonesia: A Sequential Explanatory Mixed-Methods Study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Developing an Integrated Bureaucratic Reform Model to Improve Public Healthcare Service Quality in Indonesia: A Sequential Explanatory Mixed-Methods Study
detail.abstract: Objective: Public healthcare facilities in Indonesia continue to experience bureaucratic challenges that may affect service quality, organizational effectiveness, and healthcare worker well-being. This study examined relationships among bureaucratic barriers, organizational culture, psychological well-being, and healthcare service quality, and developed a proposed integrated bureaucratic reform framework.Methods: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods study was conducted in Indonesian healthcare facilities. The quantitative phase included 220 healthcare professionals and service users who completed structured questionnaires, which were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson's correlation, and multiple linear regression. The qualitative phase involved interviews and focus group discussions with 15 healthcare professionals, managers, and stakeholders. Thematic analysis contextualized and explained the quantitative findings.Results: Bureaucratic barriers were negatively correlated with healthcare service quality (r = −0.57, p < 0.01), organizational culture (r = −0.52, p < 0.01), and psychological well-being (r = −0.48, p < 0.01). Organizational culture and psychological well-being were positively correlated with service quality (r = 0.69 and r = 0.64; p < 0.01). Regression analysis showed that bureaucratic barriers negatively predicted service quality (β = −0.301, p < 0.001), whereas organizational culture (β = 0.392, p < 0.001) and psychological well-being (β = 0.271, p < 0.001) were positive predictors. The model explained 58% of the variance in service quality. Qualitative findings highlighted repetitive documentation, fragmented coordination, manual reporting, limited digital integration, and inadequate institutional support.Conclusion: Bureaucratic reform in Indonesian public healthcare should integrate administrative simplification, a supportive organizational culture, digital governance, workforce well-being, and balanced accountability to strengthen responsive, human-centered services.

title: Optimizing Regret

detail.title: Optimizing Regret
detail.abstract: Building on the identity that expected regret equals the covariance between costs and decisions, this paper develops the complete derivative theory of the covariance regret functional. We derive the Gâteaux derivative, showing that the universal steepest-descent direction is the contrarian policy-(c-c), while ascent yields momentum. For linear policies π(c) = Ac + b, the gradient is the cost covariance matrix Σ c , with a zero Hessian implying boundary-optimal solutions such as the minimum-variance portfolio. We extend to constrained optimization, signgradient duality between regret minimization and alpha maximization, finite-sample convergence bounds paralleling Thompson Sampling, and gradient-descent algorithms requiring only input observations, with applications to portfolio tilting and LLM-based allocation strategies.

title: Rethinking Information Asymmetry in Markets Shaped by Artificial Intelligence: Algorithmic Capability, Informational Advantage, and Market Power
affiliations: Universitas Pelita Harapan - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: Rethinking Information Asymmetry in Markets Shaped by Artificial Intelligence: Algorithmic Capability, Informational Advantage, and Market Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual study did not involve human participants, patient data, animal subjects, or identifiable personal information. Therefore, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence changes competition not only by increasing the volume and speed of information processing but also by altering which firms can convert data into economically actionable knowledge. Existing research explains transactional information asymmetry, organizational artificial intelligence capability, and algorithmic market power largely in separate theoretical streams. This conceptual article integrates information economics and Industrial Organization to explain how these phenomena are connected.
